The fix is structural, for example processing commits in smaller batches or placing key items at the start and end. A fails because temperature adds randomness across the whole output and would not single out the middle of the sequence. C fails because the stem says the source messages are equally detailed throughout, so sparse input is ruled out. D fails because the context window is not full, so no compaction or summarisation has fired, and summarisation would hit the oldest commits first, not the middle ones.

questions.stem: A docs team has Claude Code generate architecture guides by synthesising source code, inline comments, commit messages, and ADRs. After several edits, the guides no longer indicate which statements came from which source. A developer later questions whether a specific architectural constraint in a guide is still valid. What approach preserves source attribution?

options.A: Instruct Claude Code to add inline footnotes to the generated prose citing the original source for each statement, and to regenerate those footnotes automatically whenever a guide is edited
options.B: Maintain structured provenance metadata for each documentation section, mapping every claim to its source file, line number, and retrieval date as machine-readable data separate from the prose
options.C: Keep all original source files unchanged in a read-only reference directory so developers can manually diff and trace any claim in a guide back to its origin whenever a constraint is questioned
options.D: Version-control the documentation so developers can run git blame on each line to trace it back to the commit that last edited it and see who changed that wording

questions.explanation: Structured provenance metadata survives editing because it is stored as data fields (e.g., JSON or YAML frontmatter) separate from the prose. When a developer questions a claim, they can trace it to the exact source file and line number. The retrieval date indicates whether the source was current when the documentation was generated.

questions.stem: Your document extraction pipeline uses a two-step process: first, it calls extract_metadata to determine the document type, then calls extract_fields with a type-specific schema. You plan to migrate this pipeline to the Message Batches API to reduce costs on a nightly run of 500 documents. What limitation of the batch API requires you to redesign this workflow?

options.A: The Message Batches API requires every request in a batch to share one identical system prompt and tool definition set, so per-document type-specific schemas are not permitted
options.B: The Message Batches API disables forced tool selection and permits only tool_choice set to auto, so you cannot compel Claude to invoke a specific extraction tool per request
options.C: The Message Batches API cannot execute a tool and feed its result back mid-request, so a two-step pipeline that runs one tool then a second tool with that result is impossible
options.D: The Message Batches API caps each submission at 100 requests per batch, so a 500-document nightly run exceeds that ceiling and cannot be sent as a single batch job

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API is fire-and-forget: it cannot execute a tool and feed the result back mid-request, so a pipeline that calls extract_metadata and then extract_fields with that result cannot run as a single batched request.

questions.stem: Your multi-agent system queries a documentation database containing thousands of technical articles organized by product area and topic. Agents currently make numerous exploratory tool calls to discover what documentation is available before performing their targeted searches, consuming significant tokens and increasing latency. What is the recommended approach to reduce these exploratory calls?

options.A: Expose a content catalog as an MCP resource that provides a browsable hierarchy of available documentation topics and article summaries
options.B: Cache the results of exploratory tool calls in a shared database that all agents query before initiating new searches
options.C: Increase each agent's max_tokens allocation to accommodate the additional exploratory tool call results
options.D: Pre-load complete summaries of all documentation articles into the system prompt for every agent invocation

questions.explanation: An MCP resource exposing a browsable catalog of topics and article summaries lets agents discover what is available by reading one resource, eliminating the many exploratory tool calls.

questions.stem: Your extraction system has the model output field-level confidence scores to route low-confidence extractions to human review. However, reviewers report that many supposedly high-confidence extractions contain errors, while some flagged low-confidence ones are correct. What is the most effective way to improve the accuracy of this routing?

options.A: Lower the confidence threshold significantly so that nearly all extractions are routed to human review
options.B: Calibrate the confidence score thresholds using a labeled validation set of known-correct extractions to align reported confidence with actual accuracy
options.C: Remove confidence scoring entirely and instead route all extractions from specific document types known to be error-prone to human review
options.D: Replace field-level confidence scores with a single document-level confidence score to simplify the routing logic

questions.explanation: Calibrating thresholds against a labeled validation set aligns reported confidence with real accuracy, so routing sends genuinely error-prone extractions to review rather than ones the model merely feels unsure about.

questions.stem: Your customer service agent connects to fetch_customer and get_order through MCP. The fetch_customer tool returns created_date as a Unix timestamp (e.g., 1718200000), while get_order returns order_date in ISO 8601 format (e.g., "2024-06-12T15:00:00Z"). The agent sometimes misinterprets these inconsistent formats when reasoning about order timelines. What is the recommended approach to ensure consistent date handling before the agent processes these results?

options.A: Implement a PostToolUse hook that normalizes date formats from both tools into a consistent representation before the agent processes the results
options.B: Modify each MCP tool server's internal implementation to always return dates in the same format
options.C: Add instructions to the system prompt telling the agent to mentally convert all dates to a single format before reasoning about timelines
options.D: Use few-shot examples in the prompt showing the agent how to correctly interpret both Unix timestamps and ISO 8601 dates

questions.explanation: A PostToolUse hook deterministically normalizes both date formats into one representation before the agent reasons over them; prompt instructions and few-shot examples cannot guarantee consistent conversion.

questions.stem: Your company policy requires that any refund exceeding $500 must be approved by a human supervisor before processing. During testing, you discover that prompt instructions alone occasionally fail to prevent the agent from calling issue_refund for amounts above the threshold. Which implementation guarantees this business rule is enforced without exception?

options.A: Include three carefully worded few-shot examples in the system prompt that demonstrate correct escalation to a supervisor whenever a refund exceeds $500
options.B: Define a maximum value constraint of 500 on the amount field in the issue_refund tool's JSON schema, relying on schema validation to reject any larger request
options.C: Strengthen the system prompt with explicit bold-emphasized instructions stating the agent must never issue any refund above $500 without prior human approval
options.D: Add a tool-call interception hook that inspects the amount on issue_refund calls, blocks those exceeding $500, and redirects the workflow to handoff_to_human

questions.explanation: Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate; a tool-call interception hook that inspects the amount and blocks/redirects calls over $500 enforces the rule deterministically every time.

questions.stem: A customer contacts your agent with a vague complaint: "Something is wrong with my account. I've been overcharged and I think someone else has accessed it." The scope of each concern is unclear until initial lookups are performed. Which task decomposition strategy is most appropriate for handling this type of open-ended, multi-concern request?

options.A: A single comprehensive prompt that includes all available customer data and asks the agent to resolve every concern in one turn
options.B: A fixed sequential pipeline that always runs fetch_customer, then get_order for the last 10 orders, then issue_refund for any billing discrepancy found
options.C: A predefined decision tree that maps each keyword in the customer's message to a specific tool call sequence
options.D: Dynamic adaptive decomposition that investigates each concern based on what is discovered at each step, generating follow-up subtasks as findings emerge

questions.explanation: When each concern's scope is unknown until you investigate, dynamic adaptive decomposition generating follow-up subtasks as findings emerge fits; fixed pipelines and keyword decision trees cannot handle the open-ended case.

questions.stem: Your team wants the customer service agent to audit the resolution quality of 50 past support tickets. Each ticket involves different product categories, refund amounts, and escalation decisions. You need the agent to evaluate each ticket's handling individually and then identify systemic patterns across the full set. Which prompt chaining pattern best supports this workflow?

options.A: Run a per-ticket evaluation pass that scores each ticket individually, then a separate synthesis pass over all evaluations to surface systemic patterns
options.B: Send all 50 tickets in a single prompt and instruct the agent to score each ticket and surface cross-ticket patterns together in one comprehensive pass
options.C: Have the agent process tickets in sequential pairs, comparing each pair for handling similarities, then aggregate all the pair comparisons into a final report
options.D: Randomly sample five representative tickets, evaluate them together in one prompt, and extrapolate those findings to characterize the remaining 45 tickets

questions.explanation: This is a map-reduce chain: evaluate each ticket individually first, then a separate synthesis pass over all evaluations surfaces systemic patterns; cramming 50 tickets into one pass loses per-ticket rigor.

questions.stem: The agent in your customer service system has a single MCP tool called manage_account that handles profile updates, password resets, subscription changes, and account deactivation. During testing, the agent frequently sends incorrect parameters because it conflates these distinct operations. What is the recommended approach to improve the agent's tool selection reliability?

options.A: Use tool_choice forced selection to always call manage_account and add a required "operation_type" enum parameter to disambiguate the intended action
options.B: Add a comprehensive description to manage_account that lists all four operations with their respective required parameters and usage conditions
options.C: Implement a PostToolUse hook that validates the parameters after each manage_account call and retries with corrected parameters if the operation type was wrong
options.D: Split manage_account into purpose-specific tools such as update_profile, reset_password, change_subscription, and deactivate_account, each with clearly defined input/output contracts

questions.explanation: A single tool spanning four distinct operations invites parameter confusion; splitting into purpose-specific tools with clear input/output contracts gives the model an unambiguous choice.

questions.stem: Within your customer service system, the agent has four well-described MCP tools: fetch_customer, get_order, issue_refund, and handoff_to_human. Despite clear tool descriptions, whenever a customer mentions the word "refund," the agent consistently calls handoff_to_human instead of issue_refund, even for straightforward cases within policy. After reviewing the configuration, you find the system prompt includes: "When a customer mentions a refund, always ensure a human is involved." What is the most likely cause of this behavior and how should it be resolved?

options.A: The issue_refund tool description lacks sufficient detail, so it should be expanded to explicitly state that it takes priority over handoff_to_human for any standard refund request that clearly falls within policy.
options.B: The tool_choice setting should be switched to forced selection of issue_refund whenever refund-related keywords appear, guaranteeing the right tool fires without relying on the model's own judgment.
options.C: The keyword-sensitive system-prompt instruction creates an unintended association that overrides the tool descriptions, so it should be rewritten to specify the precise conditions that require human involvement.
options.D: The handoff_to_human and issue_refund descriptions overlap too closely, so both tools should be renamed to more distinctive labels that make the agent's choice between them unambiguous.

questions.explanation: The keyword-triggered instruction creates an association that overrides the tool descriptions; rewrite it to specify the precise conditions that actually require human involvement.

questions.stem: Currently, your customer service agent has access to fetch_customer and get_order, but both tools have minimal one-line descriptions: "Fetches customer data" and "Gets order information." When a customer asks about a recent purchase, the agent inconsistently alternates between calling fetch_customer and get_order. What is the primary reason for this unreliable tool selection?

options.A: The model cannot reliably choose between two similar tools unless tool_choice is set to forced selection, which pins the first call and removes the ambiguity
options.B: The agent's context window is exhausted by conversation history, leaving too little room to load both tool definitions, so selection becomes random
options.C: The two tool names are too similar in length and structure, so the model confuses them at selection time regardless of their descriptions
options.D: Tool descriptions are the primary signal the model uses to select tools, and one-line descriptions do not convey when fetch_customer applies versus get_order

questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary signal the model uses to select tools; one-line descriptions do not give it enough to know when fetch_customer applies versus get_order, so selection is unreliable.

questions.stem: The get_order tool in your customer service agent sometimes fails in two distinct ways: a temporary database timeout that resolves on retry, and a business policy violation when a customer requests a refund on a non-returnable item. Currently, both failures return a generic message: "Operation failed." Why is returning structured error metadata with distinct error categories critical for these two scenarios?

options.A: Structured error metadata is valuable chiefly because it reduces token usage in the conversation history, swapping verbose failure strings for compact codes the agent can parse and store more cheaply
options.B: Structured error metadata exists primarily for backend logging and observability dashboards, feeding monitoring systems and alerts without changing how the agent reasons about or responds to the customer
options.C: The MCP protocol requires every tool error to carry a standardized error-category field, and the agent is prohibited from continuing the conversation until that required category is present in the response
options.D: Without metadata distinguishing transient errors from business-rule violations, the agent cannot tell whether to retry the call or explain the policy, causing wasted retries or poor customer communication

questions.explanation: Distinct error categories tell the agent whether a failure is transient (retry) or a business-rule violation (explain the policy); a generic failure message leaves it guessing, wasting retries or communicating poorly.

questions.stem: Your structured data extraction system processes real estate listing documents. When listings describe property size with informal terms like "spacious" or "generous open-plan living area" instead of exact measurements, the model frequently fabricates numeric square footage values. Which approach would most effectively reduce these hallucinated values while preserving extraction accuracy for documents that contain explicit measurements?

options.A: Making the square_footage field required in the schema and adding a post-extraction validation step that rejects any non-numeric value before the record is saved
options.B: Adding a system prompt instruction telling the model to only extract square footage values it is highly certain about and to otherwise leave the field blank
options.C: Providing few-shot examples that return null for square footage when documents use informal descriptions, alongside examples that extract explicit numeric measurements
options.D: Removing the square_footage field from the schema entirely and instead storing the property's raw size wording as free text in a separate notes field

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples that return null for informal descriptions and extract explicit measurements teach the model the boundary between stated and unstated data, cutting fabrication without hurting recall on real numbers.

questions.stem: You need to locate all migration script files across a large monorepo. These files follow the naming convention YYYYMMDD_description.sql and are distributed across multiple service directories at various nesting levels. Which built-in tool is the most appropriate choice for this task?

options.A: Grep, searching file contents for SQL migration keywords like CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE
options.B: Bash, running a custom script that parses directory listings and filters by file extension
options.C: Glob, using a pattern like **/*_*.sql to match migration file paths across all directories
options.D: Read, loading each service directory to manually scan for migration files

questions.explanation: Glob matches file paths by pattern, so a glob like **/*_*.sql finds migration files across all nesting levels; Grep searches contents, which is not what is needed here.

questions.stem: When a web search subagent in a multi-agent research pipeline encounters a database timeout and returns the generic message "search unavailable" to the coordinator, what is the primary problem this creates?

options.A: It prevents the coordinator from distinguishing a transient timeout from a permanent access restriction, so it cannot choose a recovery strategy
options.B: It causes the coordinator to immediately terminate the entire research workflow and discard every partial result the other subagents already produced
options.C: It causes every other subagent to halt processing until a human operator manually clears the fault from the shared task queue
options.D: It forces the coordinator to retry the identical query on a fixed schedule until the search service eventually recovers

questions.explanation: A generic "search unavailable" hides whether the failure is a transient timeout (retry) or a permanent restriction (try another source), so the coordinator cannot pick the right recovery strategy.

questions.stem: While implementing the orchestrator agent's agentic loop for the research platform, a developer decides to check whether the assistant's response text contains the phrase "research complete" to determine when the loop should terminate. Why is this approach considered an anti-pattern?

options.A: It prevents the model from emitting tool_use content blocks in later iterations, since scanning the response text consumes the assistant turn early
options.B: It forces the model to always emit the phrase before invoking any tools, adding unnecessary latency and token overhead to every loop iteration
options.C: It causes the API to raise an error because assistant response text cannot be inspected until the entire conversation has fully completed
options.D: It relies on parsing non-deterministic natural language instead of the reliable stop_reason field, producing inconsistent termination behavior

questions.explanation: Parsing free-text for a phrase like "research complete" is brittle because model output is non-deterministic; the stop_reason field is the reliable termination signal.

questions.stem: In the research automation platform, the orchestrator agent runs an agentic loop that sends requests to Claude, receives responses, and decides whether to continue or stop. What mechanism does the loop use to determine whether it should execute another tool call or present the final response?

options.A: The loop keeps a running count of the tool calls made and halts automatically once it reaches a predefined maximum iteration limit
options.B: The system prompt defines a special termination keyword that the model emits in its text output once it has finished all processing
options.C: The model returns a boolean "continue" field inside its structured JSON response body, which the loop evaluates at the end of every iteration
options.D: The stop_reason field in the API response reads "tool_use" when the model wants to call a tool and "end_turn" when it considers the task complete

questions.explanation: The loop reads stop_reason: "tool_use" means Claude wants to run a tool (continue), "end_turn" means it is done (present the final response).

questions.stem: After the web search agent executes a tool and receives results during its agentic loop, the developer appends the tool results to the conversation history before sending the next API request. What is the primary purpose of including these results in the conversation?

options.A: To enable the API to cache the tool results server-side for faster processing of subsequent requests
options.B: To satisfy an API validation rule that requires strictly alternating message roles in the conversation array
options.C: To allow the API to deduplicate repeated tool calls and reduce unnecessary computation
options.D: To enable the model to incorporate the new information into its reasoning and determine the appropriate next action in the loop

questions.explanation: Appending tool results lets the model see what its call returned and reason about the next action; the stateless API needs the full history each turn.

questions.stem: After the coordinator collects web search results, it invokes the findings synthesis agent to combine all research. However, the synthesis output shows no awareness of the previously gathered search findings, even though they are clearly present in the coordinator's conversation history. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The coordinator's context window exceeded its limit, causing the search results to be silently dropped before the synthesis agent was invoked
options.B: The search results were returned in an encoding format that the synthesis agent cannot process
options.C: The synthesis agent's system prompt contains an instruction that explicitly excludes externally sourced data
options.D: Subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history, so the search findings were never part of the synthesis agent's context

questions.explanation: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history, so unless the coordinator explicitly passes the search findings into the synthesis agent's prompt, they were never in its context.

questions.stem: A user submits a simple factual question to the research automation platform that can be fully answered with a single web lookup. The coordinator has access to the web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report generation subagents. How should the coordinator handle this query differently than a complex multi-faceted research topic?

options.A: Forward the question straight to the user interface without involving any subagents, since the coordinator can answer simple factual queries on its own
options.B: Route the query to the synthesis agent first so it can decide which of the other subagents are needed and coordinate the final response
options.C: Invoke the full pipeline of all four subagents to guarantee consistent, thorough output regardless of the actual complexity of the query
options.D: Analyze the query requirements and invoke only the web search agent, skipping document analysis, synthesis, and report generation as unneeded

questions.explanation: The coordinator should analyze the query and invoke only the subagents it needs, a single web lookup for a simple fact, rather than always running the full pipeline.

questions.stem: The coordinator agent in the research platform is about to invoke the findings synthesis agent using a stateless agent call (so subagents do not inherit prior conversation context). Both the web search agent and the document analysis agent have already returned their results. How should the coordinator provide these prior findings to the synthesis agent?

options.A: Pass only a brief thematic summary to keep the synthesis agent's context lean and avoid exceeding token limits
options.B: Include the complete findings from both agents directly in the synthesis agent's prompt so it has full access to all gathered information
options.C: Store the findings in an external database and give the synthesis agent credentials to query the results on its own
options.D: Instruct the synthesis agent to re-invoke the web search and document analysis agents independently to collect the information it needs

questions.explanation: A stateless synthesis agent only knows what is in its prompt, so include the complete findings from both agents directly; a lean summary or external store would starve it of the information it needs to synthesize.

questions.stem: The document analysis agent returns its findings as narrative text that blends source citations into flowing paragraphs. When the coordinator passes these results to the synthesis agent, the final report frequently contains misattributed or missing source references. Which change to the inter-agent data format would best address this problem?

options.A: Instruct the synthesis agent to re-read each source document and independently reverify every citation against the original text before writing the report
options.B: Have the document analysis agent return structured findings that separate each claim from its source metadata: URLs, document names, and page numbers
options.C: Add a post-processing step that uses regular expressions to extract and reattach the citations from the narrative paragraphs once synthesis is fully complete
options.D: Increase the synthesis agent context window budget so it can hold the entire narrative passage in memory and retain citation details without any truncation

questions.explanation: Returning findings as structured data that separates each claim from its source metadata (URLs, document names, page numbers) preserves attribution through synthesis; narrative prose blends citations and loses the mapping.

questions.stem: In the research platform, the report generation agent must only produce a final report after the synthesis agent has confirmed that all research areas have adequate coverage. A developer enforces this ordering with a system prompt instruction telling the report agent to wait for synthesis confirmation. Why is a programmatic prerequisite gate a better choice?

options.A: Programmatic gates execute faster than prompt-based instructions, so the report agent produces its final output with lower pipeline latency
options.B: Prompt instructions are evaluated only once at session start and stop applying once the report agent begins issuing its own tool calls
options.C: Programmatic gates enforce ordering deterministically, while prompt instructions carry a non-zero failure rate and cannot guarantee compliance
options.D: System prompts cannot reference other agents, so the report agent has no reliable way to learn that the synthesis step has finished

questions.explanation: A programmatic prerequisite gate enforces the ordering deterministically; prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate and cannot guarantee the report waits for synthesis confirmation.

questions.stem: A customer support agent calls the process_refund MCP tool, which fails because the requested refund amount exceeds the customer's original order total. Currently the tool returns a generic "Operation failed" message, preventing the agent from explaining the issue to the customer. How should the tool's error response be restructured to enable appropriate handling?

options.A: Return an error with errorCategory: "transient", isRetryable: true, and a description suggesting the agent retry with the same parameters after a delay
options.B: Return a successful empty result with a warning field embedded in the response content indicating the amount was too high
options.C: Return an error with errorCategory: "permission", isRetryable: true, and a description indicating the operation requires supervisor-level access
options.D: Return an error with errorCategory: "validation", isRetryable: false, and a description explaining the refund amount exceeds the order total

questions.explanation: The failure is a permanent business-rule violation, so the structured error should be errorCategory "validation", isRetryable false, with a description the agent can relay; retrying or claiming a permission issue would be wrong.

questions.stem: A new engineer on the team reports that Claude Code is not following the project's API naming conventions during code generation, even though other engineers on the same repository see the conventions applied correctly. What is the most effective first diagnostic step to identify the cause of this inconsistency?

options.A: Move all project configuration from .claude/rules/ into a single root-level CLAUDE.md to simplify the file structure
options.B: Reinstall Claude Code on the engineer's machine to clear any corrupted cached configurations
options.C: Ask the engineer to run the /memory command to verify which memory files are currently loaded in their session
options.D: Add the API naming conventions as inline comments in every source file so Claude Code reads them directly

questions.explanation: Running /memory shows which memory files are actually loaded in the engineer's session, pinpointing whether the convention file is being picked up; that is the right first diagnostic before reinstalling or restructuring.

questions.stem: Your team wants to enforce a universal rule that all generated TypeScript code must use named exports instead of default exports. This standard should apply automatically every time Claude Code writes or modifies any TypeScript file in the project. Where should this convention be defined?

options.A: In a skill file under .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md that engineers invoke on demand before writing code
options.B: In a user-scoped command under ~/.claude/commands/ that each developer runs at the start of their session
options.C: In a custom slash command stored in .claude/commands/ that developers must remember to call before each task
options.D: In the project-level CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules/ file so it is always loaded for every interaction

questions.explanation: A universal convention that must apply automatically to every TypeScript edit belongs in project CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules/ file, which is always loaded; commands and skills require manual or on-demand invocation.

questions.stem: One of your engineers creates a slash command that scaffolds a new REST API endpoint with standardized error handling and validation. The team agrees this command should be available to all developers working on the project without requiring any manual setup on individual machines. Which configuration achieves this goal?

options.A: Add the command as a SKILL.md file in ~/.claude/skills/ with argument-hint frontmatter configured
options.B: Place the command file in the project's .claude/commands/ directory and commit it to version control
options.C: Place the command file in ~/.claude/commands/ on the engineer's machine and share the file path in a wiki
options.D: Define the command inline within the root CLAUDE.md file using @import syntax

questions.explanation: Placing the command in the project's .claude/commands/ directory and committing it makes it available to every developer on clone or pull with no per-machine setup.

questions.stem: Your team must replace the project's logging library across 60+ source files. The migration involves auditing current usage patterns, selecting appropriate replacement APIs for different log levels, and applying consistent changes. What is the recommended workflow for completing this task in Claude Code?

options.A: Start 60 separate Claude Code sessions in parallel, one per file, each using direct execution independently
options.B: Use plan mode for the full duration of the migration, including both the investigation phase and every individual file modification
options.C: Start with plan mode to audit usage patterns and design the migration strategy, then switch to direct execution to apply the changes according to the plan
options.D: Use direct execution for the entire migration, processing each file one at a time without any upfront investigation

questions.explanation: Start in plan mode to audit usage and design the migration strategy, then switch to direct execution to apply the changes; plan the investigation up front, execute the mechanical edits after.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to fix a bug where a single function throws an error when receiving a null input. The stack trace clearly identifies the file and line number, and the fix requires adding one conditional check. Which mode should the engineer use for this task?

options.A: Plan mode, because every code change benefits from an investigation phase before implementation
options.B: Direct execution combined with the Explore subagent to verify no other functions have the same issue before making the change
options.C: Plan mode, because null handling requires evaluating multiple valid implementation strategies across the codebase
options.D: Direct execution, because the task is well-scoped with a clear fix in a single file and does not require architectural exploration

questions.explanation: A well-scoped, single-file fix with a known location and a one-line change is ideal for direct execution; plan mode's investigation phase would be unnecessary overhead.

questions.stem: Your team asks Claude Code to transform legacy configuration files from an INI format into YAML. Despite detailed prose instructions describing the mapping rules, Claude Code produces inconsistent key naming and indentation across different files. What is the most effective technique to resolve this inconsistency?

options.A: Increase the length of the prose instructions by adding more detailed paragraphs explaining each mapping rule
options.B: Add a general instruction in CLAUDE.md that says "always be consistent when transforming configuration formats"
options.C: Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples showing the exact transformation from specific INI sections to the expected YAML output
options.D: Switch to plan mode and ask Claude Code to outline its transformation approach before applying any changes

questions.explanation: Concrete input/output examples pin down the exact transformation when prose has failed; 2-3 INI-to-YAML pairs resolve the key-naming and indentation ambiguity.

questions.stem: Your team is using Claude Code to implement a new CSV parsing module that must handle complex edge cases, including quoted delimiters, multiline fields, and malformed rows. Requirements are well-defined but numerous. Which approach best supports iterative refinement of the implementation?

options.A: Generate the full implementation with Claude Code, then manually run each edge case yourself and file a separate bug report for every individual failure you find along the way
options.B: Describe every edge case in one detailed prompt and ask Claude Code to generate both the complete implementation and its full accompanying test suite together in a single pass
options.C: Implement the module first without any tests, then ask Claude Code to review its own output for issues in the same session and refine it based on whatever it reports back
options.D: Write a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases, and malformed input first, then iterate by sharing the failing tests with Claude Code to guide its corrections

questions.explanation: Writing the test suite first and iterating by feeding failures back to Claude gives a concrete, executable target for each edge case; this is test-driven refinement.

questions.stem: While updating a large configuration file, Claude Code's Edit tool fails with an error indicating the target text appears in multiple locations within the file. The specific section that needs modification contains boilerplate text identical to several other sections. What is the recommended fallback approach?

options.A: Split the configuration file into smaller files so that each section contains unique text for Edit to match
options.B: Use Bash to run a sed command that targets the specific line number for replacement
options.C: Retry the Edit tool with a larger context window setting to improve text matching precision
options.D: Use Read to load the full file contents, apply the modification, and then use Write to save the complete updated file

questions.explanation: When Edit cannot uniquely match because the target text is duplicated boilerplate, fall back to Read the full file, modify in memory, and Write it back.

questions.stem: A team provides four few-shot examples showing Claude how to distinguish acceptable defensive null-check patterns from genuine error-handling bugs during code review. After deployment, the agent correctly identifies a problematic error-handling pattern in a codebase written in a different language than any of the examples. What best explains this behavior?

options.A: The model matched the flagged code against language-specific review rules it memorized from pre-training, applying syntax patterns unique to that language rather than transferred judgment
options.B: The few-shot examples conveyed the underlying judgment criteria for evaluating error handling, which the model generalized to a structurally similar but previously unseen pattern
options.C: The model defaulted to flagging any unfamiliar construct as suspicious because it did not match the exact acceptable patterns shown in the four few-shot examples it was given
options.D: The model decomposed the novel pattern into discrete sub-patterns that each matched literal tokens from the few-shot examples, then reassembled them to reach its conclusion

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples teach the underlying judgment criteria, which generalise to structurally similar, previously unseen cases (even in a different language) — not literal matching of the example patterns.

questions.stem: A React table component renders correctly in most cases, but for rows with very long labels the cells overlap and a tooltip gets clipped. There is no console error or exception — it simply renders wrong. You want Claude Code to fix it, and the component source is available in the repo. What is the most effective way to communicate the problem?

options.A: Take a screenshot of the component in its broken state, along with the reproduction steps, so Claude Code can see exactly how it renders.
options.B: Paste the component's full source code and describe the misalignment in the prompt.
options.C: Write a precise prose description of the glitch — which elements overlap, by roughly how many pixels, and where the tooltip is cut off.
options.D: Copy the browser console output and stack trace into the prompt for Claude Code to diagnose.

questions.explanation: The defect lives only in the rendered output — the source 'looks fine' and there is no exception to read — so a screenshot of the broken state (with repro steps) is the highest-fidelity and only faithful way to convey it. A screenshot is right here not because the task is 'UI' but because the information exists nowhere else: pasting the code (B) conveys little when the fault isn't legible in the source, a stack trace (D) is empty for a pure render bug that throws nothing, and prose (C) can't reliably encode a spatial/visual glitch.

questions.stem: Your CI pipeline runs `claude -p "review this PR"` on every push. Occasionally the agent gets into a long tool-use loop, inflating both CI duration and API spend. You need each run to be bounded so it can never overspend a set dollar limit. What is the best approach?

options.A: Use `--max-turns N` to cap the loop, and after the run parse `total_cost_usd` from `--output-format json` to fail the build if it exceeded the budget.
options.B: Use `--max-turns N` together with `--max-budget-usd X`, so the run stops itself as soon as either the turn count or the spend ceiling is reached.
options.C: Wrap the command in a shell `timeout 120` so the process is killed if it runs too long.
options.D: Switch to `--model haiku` to lower the per-token cost.

questions.explanation: Only `--max-budget-usd X` enforces the dollar limit during the run — it stops before exceeding it — while `--max-turns N` bounds the loop. A is the tempting near-miss: it uses real flags and does track cost, but the `total_cost_usd` check is post-hoc, so the money is already spent by the time the build reads the JSON; it detects overspend rather than preventing it, failing the stem's 'never overspend' requirement. C bounds wall-clock seconds, not turns or dollars, and kills the run ungracefully. D lowers the per-token rate but not the total — a runaway loop still overruns.

questions.stem: You run a nightly pipeline that extracts structured fields from 8,000 insurance claim documents through the Messages API. Every request sends an identical shared prefix — a large system prompt with policy rules, the JSON extraction schema as tool definitions, and 6 few-shot examples (~3,500 tokens combined) — followed by the individual claim document (~1,200 tokens each). You want to cut input costs with prompt caching. How should you apply cache_control?

options.A: Add a cache_control breakpoint every 200 documents so the cache is rebuilt periodically, keeping the shared prefix warm and preventing the cached entry from expiring partway through the batch.
options.B: Place cache_control on each claim document’s content block so every document is cached individually and can be reused when a similar claim recurs later in the batch.
options.C: Place a single cache_control breakpoint at the end of the shared prefix (system prompt, tool/schema definitions, and few-shot examples), leaving each claim document after it uncached.
options.D: Enable the 1-hour cache TTL so the cached prefix survives the full 24-hour batch window, guaranteeing a cache hit on every one of the 8,000 claim documents processed.

questions.explanation: Prompt caching is a prefix match: one cache_control breakpoint caches everything before it (render order tools → system → messages) and leaves everything after it uncached. A single breakpoint at the end of the shared prefix caches the ~3,500-token system + tool/schema + few-shot block once and reuses it across all 8,000 documents, while each unique claim document sits after the breakpoint and is billed fresh. B caches unique per-request content that is never reused, paying the ~1.25x write premium for nothing. A misunderstands caching — it is prefix-based, not a periodic 'refresh' every N documents. D is factually wrong: the maximum cache TTL is 1 hour, not 24 hours, and hits are never 'guaranteed' (a steady request stream refreshes the TTL on each hit to keep the prefix warm, but that is not what the option claims).

questions.stem: A customer support agent resolves what it can autonomously, but for out-of-scope cases it escalates to a human. The human agent picks up the ticket in a separate tool and has no access to the conversation history. What should the agent include in the escalation payload so the human can continue effectively?

options.A: A short note such as "Customer wants a refund" plus the customer's name and email, so the human can pull up the account and re-read the full ticket themselves.
options.B: The entire raw conversation transcript pasted verbatim, including timestamps and system messages, so the human loses no detail and can reconstruct the events.
options.C: A structured handoff: verified customer ID, root-cause diagnosis, resolution steps already tried and their outcomes, the refund amount, and a recommended next action.
options.D: A sentiment summary with a politeness score and an urgency rating, so the human knows how upset the customer is and how gently to open the reply.

questions.explanation: A human with no context cannot continue efficiently from a vague note, and a raw transcript forces them to re-derive the situation. A structured handoff puts everything actionable in one place—who the customer is (verified), what is actually wrong (root cause), what has already been tried, the financial stakes, and the recommended action—so the human resumes rather than restarts. Sentiment/politeness scores don't help resolve the case; the issue's substance does.

questions.stem: Your agent runs a tool-use loop and already checks stop_reason correctly (tool_use → run tool and continue, end_turn → return to the user). The team is worried about a bug or pathological input causing a runaway loop that burns tokens. What safeguard should you add?

options.A: Replace the stop_reason check with a fixed iteration cap, since a hard turn limit stops the loop more reliably than model signals.
options.B: Parse the assistant's text each turn for phrases like 'done' or 'finished' and stop the loop as soon as such a completion cue appears.
options.C: No safeguard is needed, because correct stop_reason handling on its own already guarantees the loop will always terminate.
options.D: Keep stop_reason as the primary completion signal and add an iteration cap as a secondary backstop for runaway loops.

questions.explanation: stop_reason is the only reliable completion signal, so it must stay primary; a cap used as the PRIMARY stop mechanism would truncate legitimate long-running tasks. But as a SECONDARY backstop, an iteration cap is a reasonable safety net for the case where a bug prevents end_turn from ever arriving. Parsing text for 'done' is unreliable (Claude may say it mid-task), and assuming termination is guaranteed ignores real failure modes.

questions.stem: A coordinator in a multi-agent research system needs to run a web-search subagent and a document-analysis subagent. The two tasks are independent and you want them to execute concurrently to reduce wall-clock time. How should the coordinator dispatch them?

options.A: Emit both Task tool calls within a single coordinator response so the SDK runs the subagents concurrently.
options.B: Issue the two Task calls in separate turns—one Task call per coordinator response.
options.C: Make one Task call listing both subagents and set a parallel: true flag on it.
options.D: Give a single subagent both jobs so there is no cross-agent coordination to manage.

questions.explanation: Multiple Task tool calls emitted in one response are launched concurrently by the SDK. Issuing them in separate turns forces sequential execution—each waits for the previous turn to complete. There is no 'parallel: true' flag listing multiple subagents in one Task call, and collapsing both jobs into one subagent defeats the point (and dilutes its focus).

questions.stem: A long code-exploration session captured tool results describing the database schema. Since then the schema has changed materially. You need to continue the work. Resuming the old session would bring back the now-stale schema tool results. What is the best way to continue?

options.A: Use --resume so all prior context and tool results are preserved and nothing is lost.
options.B: Use fork_session from a point before the schema changed and continue from there.
options.C: Start a fresh session and inject a summary of the still-valid findings, discarding the stale tool results.
options.D: Resume the old session and instruct the agent to ignore the outdated schema results.

questions.explanation: Stale tool results actively mislead the agent, and telling it to 'ignore' them is probabilistic—it may still reason from them. A fresh session with an explicitly injected summary of the valid findings gives a clean context free of the outdated state. This differs from the case where only a few FILES changed—there, --resume plus a targeted note about the changed files is correct because the rest of the context is still accurate.

questions.stem: In a multi-agent system, the web-search subagent runs its query successfully but finds no matching articles. How should the tool return this outcome to the coordinator?

options.A: Return an error with a retryable flag so the coordinator automatically reruns the search until articles are found.
options.B: Return an empty results array with no status field, letting the coordinator infer on its own that the search finished.
options.C: Raise an exception describing the empty response so the coordinator escalates the query to a human reviewer for triage.
options.D: Return a success result: isError:false, empty results array, and a message noting no articles were found.

questions.explanation: A successful search that finds nothing is a valid empty result, not a failure. Returning an error makes the coordinator retry a query that worked fine. Returning a silent empty array is ambiguous—the coordinator can't distinguish 'searched, found nothing' from 'something broke.' An explicit isError:false plus a message tells the coordinator the search succeeded and there is simply no data, so it can move on.

questions.stem: You connect several MCP servers to Claude Code, exposing dozens of tools. With MCP tool search enabled (the default), what actually loads into the context window when the session starts?

options.A: The full tool definitions (names, descriptions, and input schemas) for every tool on every connected server, at connection time.
options.B: Only the tool names plus each server's instructions; the full tool definitions are deferred and fetched on demand when a tool is actually needed.
options.C: Only the tools you have used in previous sessions; the rest are never loaded.
options.D: Tools load lazily on demand, but server instructions are never loaded into context.

questions.explanation: With tool search on by default, session start loads only lightweight tool names plus server instructions; full schemas are deferred and pulled in on demand. This keeps the context lean and preserves selection quality, which degrades once dozens of full definitions compete for attention. Loading every definition upfront is the old behavior (tool search off). Discovery still happens for all tools—only the loading of their full definitions into context is deferred.

questions.stem: You connect a small, trusted set of MCP tools and want their full schemas loaded into context immediately at startup—no on-demand fetching—so there is zero mid-task latency from tool search. How do you configure this?

options.A: Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true to force all schemas to load upfront.
options.B: Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto, which always loads all schemas regardless of their size.
options.C: Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false to disable deferral and load all tool definitions upfront.
options.D: It cannot be changed—deferred loading is always on when tool search is available.

questions.explanation: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false turns tool search off, so all tool definitions load upfront at startup. Unset or =true defers (tool search on). =auto loads schemas upfront only if they fit within a threshold (~10% of the context window by default; auto:N sets a custom percentage) and otherwise defers—so it does not 'always' load everything. Deferral is therefore configurable, not fixed.

questions.stem: A Model Context Protocol client connects to an MCP server. In what order do the protocol interactions occur across the connection's lifetime?

options.A: initialize to negotiate capabilities, after which the client re-sends tools/list at the start of every turn to refresh the tool set before each tools/call, since the server never signals changes on its own.
options.B: tools/list first to discover what the server offers, then initialize to negotiate capabilities once the tool set is known, then tools/call whenever a specific tool is actually invoked.
options.C: initialize, then tools/call directly, since tool definitions come back inline with the first call's response, so a separate tools/list discovery step is never needed at all.
options.D: initialize for capability exchange, then discovery at connect time via tools/list, resources/list and prompts/list, then tools/call on demand, then a list_changed notification when the set changes.

questions.explanation: Per the MCP specification the connection begins with an initialize capability handshake; discovery via tools/list (and resources/list, prompts/list) happens AFTER initialize, at connect time; tools are then invoked on demand with tools/call; and when the available set changes the server sends a list_changed notification. Discovery never precedes initialize (rules out listing first), the client does not re-request the list every turn, and calls never come before the handshake.

questions.stem: You are exposing database table schemas through an MCP server. There are many tables, all retrieved the same way—by table name. How should you model this as MCP resources?

options.A: Define one templated resource whose URI takes a {name} parameter (e.g. db://tables/{name}/schema) to cover every table.
options.B: Register a separate direct resource with its own static URI for each table, so every schema is listed as an individually fixed object.
options.C: Expose a tool that returns a schema by name, since MCP resources are strictly static and cannot accept URI parameters.
options.D: Concatenate all table schemas into a single direct resource returned as one combined blob for clients to fetch at once.

questions.explanation: A templated resource uses a URI template with a parameter to represent an entire family of items with one definition; a direct resource is for a single fixed object. One template is far better than one static resource per table. Resources can be parameterized, so the tool workaround is unnecessary, and merging every schema into one blob destroys per-table addressability.

questions.stem: A synthesis subagent is supposed to combine findings the other agents already gathered, but it repeatedly calls the web-search tools itself instead of synthesizing, going outside its specialization. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Add a firmly worded system-prompt rule forbidding the synthesis agent from ever calling the web-search tools.
options.B: Keep the synthesis agent's full tool access but lower its temperature so it reliably chooses to synthesize.
options.C: Restrict the synthesis agent's allowedTools to only synthesis tools such as summarize and verify_fact.
options.D: Fold the synthesis step back into the coordinator so no separate agent exists that could call search tools.

questions.explanation: allowedTools is a hard, configuration-level restriction—an agent simply cannot call a tool that isn't in its list. A prompt instruction is probabilistic and can be ignored. Exposing every tool degrades selection reliability regardless of temperature, and collapsing the specialized synthesis role into the coordinator throws away the separation of concerns the architecture depends on.

questions.stem: An agent must always return structured data by calling one of several extraction tools, but it sometimes replies with a plain-text summary instead of calling any tool. The document type varies, so you cannot know in advance which extraction tool is correct. How do you guarantee a tool call?

options.A: Set tool_choice: "auto" and add an instruction telling Claude to always use a tool.
options.B: Set tool_choice: { type: "tool", name: "extract_generic" } to force one specific extraction tool every time.
options.C: Add few-shot examples that each end in a tool call to nudge the model toward calling tools.
options.D: Set tool_choice: "any", which forces Claude to call one of the tools while letting it choose which.

questions.explanation: tool_choice: "any" requires the model to emit a tool call but leaves the choice of WHICH tool to the model—correct when the right tool depends on the (unknown) document type. "auto" permits a text reply, so instructions on top of it are still probabilistic. Forcing one specific tool is wrong when the document type varies. Few-shot nudging is probabilistic, not a guarantee.

questions.stem: A developer wants to experiment with a personal MCP server without affecting teammates and without committing anything to the shared project repository. Where should the server be configured?

options.A: In the project's .mcp.json so it's available in the repo.
options.B: In ~/.claude.json, which is user-scoped and never committed to git.
options.C: In the project's .mcp.json, but add that file to .gitignore.
options.D: In .mcp.json on a separate personal branch of the repository.

questions.explanation: Project-scoped .mcp.json is shared with the whole team through git. A personal, experimental server belongs in the user-scoped ~/.claude.json, which applies only to that developer and is not part of any repository. Gitignoring the project file or using a personal branch are fragile workarounds that still put team-shared configuration in the wrong scope.

questions.stem: You are designing an MCP server that needs to expose three things: (a) an operation that writes records to a system, (b) read-only reference data the model should be able to pull into context, and (c) a canned multi-step workflow a user triggers deliberately. Which primitive fits each?

options.A: Expose all three as tools, since tools are the only MCP primitive the model can actually invoke, and let it choose which to call based on their descriptions.
options.B: Write operation → tool; reference data → tool, so the model can query it on demand; workflow → resource the user loads to kick off the steps.
options.C: Write operation → tool (model-controlled); reference data → resource (app-controlled, read-only); workflow → prompt (user-controlled), a Claude Code slash command.
options.D: Write operation → prompt (a user-approved template); reference data → resource (read-only); workflow → tool the model fires whenever it judges the steps are needed.

questions.explanation: MCP has three primitives with different initiators: tools are model-controlled actions, resources are app-controlled read-only context, and prompts are user-controlled templates (in Claude Code invoked as /mcp__server__prompt slash commands). Exposing read-only data as a tool forces needless exploratory tool calls, and modeling a user-triggered workflow as a tool lets the model fire it at the wrong moment. Matching each to the right primitive puts control in the right hands.

questions.stem: A CI script runs `claude -p` to generate release notes. The default coding-assistant personality keeps volunteering to run tests and improve code—its whole identity is wrong for this non-coding task. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Use --append-system-prompt with instructions like "do not suggest running tests or improving code."
options.B: Add a CLAUDE.md that tells the model not to behave like a coding assistant.
options.C: Lower the temperature so the model stops volunteering suggestions.
options.D: Use --system-prompt to replace the default system prompt entirely with one written for release-note generation.

questions.explanation: When the default identity is fundamentally unsuited to the task, replace it wholesale with --system-prompt. Appending negative instructions only patches symptoms probabilistically, and a CLAUDE.md or a temperature change doesn't remove the built-in coding-assistant persona. Note that replacing also discards the default tool guidance and safety framing, so you take responsibility for those in your replacement prompt.

questions.stem: Your CI code-review runs Claude as a normal coding assistant. You want to add exactly one extra rule—"also flag missing error handling"—while keeping Claude's full coding-assistant behavior and its default tool guidance. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Rewrite the default system prompt inline to include the rule alongside tool guidance.
options.B: Use --system-prompt containing only the new rule, replacing the default prompt.
options.C: Use --append-system-prompt to layer the rule on top of the default system prompt.
options.D: Put the rule in the repository's CLAUDE.md so the CI run picks it up automatically.

questions.explanation: --append-system-prompt layers your rule on top of the default while preserving the coding-assistant identity and tool guidance you still want. --system-prompt (or rewriting the default) would discard all of that base behavior. Putting the rule in CLAUDE.md would change behavior for every session and every developer, not just this CI review—append is the targeted, deterministic lever for adding one rule to this run.

questions.stem: You maintain a full custom agent prompt in `base-agent.txt` and a separate set of output-formatting rules in `style-rules.txt`, both under version control. In a `claude -p` script you want the agent to use the custom base AND apply the formatting rules on top of it. Which invocation does this?

options.A: Pass both files using two --system-prompt-file flags.
options.B: Concatenate the two files and pass the result with a single --append-system-prompt-file.
options.C: Use --system-prompt-file base-agent.txt together with --append-system-prompt-file style-rules.txt.
options.D: Inline both files' contents via --system-prompt, since the -file variants only work in interactive mode.

questions.explanation: The -file variants read the prompt text from a file. --system-prompt-file sets the base identity from base-agent.txt (replacing the default), and --append-system-prompt-file layers style-rules.txt on top of that chosen base—applying both. Two replacement flags don't compose (there is only one base identity). Appending both files to the default (rather than replacing the base) would keep the default coding-assistant persona instead of using base-agent.txt as the base — a different result. The -file flags work in -p mode too, not only interactively.

questions.stem: A shell script invokes `claude -p` hundreds of times in a loop. Each invocation is slow to start because it auto-discovers CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, plugins, and MCP servers. The task only needs to read and write files and run Bash. How do you speed up the scripted calls?

options.A: Use --strict-mcp-config to stop loading MCP servers, which removes the bulk of the slow per-call startup overhead.
options.B: Use --disable-slash-commands to skip discovery of commands, skills, and hooks so that each call starts faster.
options.C: Delete CLAUDE.md and the .claude directory before each run so that nothing is auto-discovered on startup.
options.D: Use --bare to skip all auto-discovery (CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, plugins, MCP), leaving Bash and file tools.

questions.explanation: --bare disables the entire auto-discovery pipeline in a single flag—hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, auto-memory, and CLAUDE.md—leaving Bash and file read/edit, which is exactly what this scripted task needs. --strict-mcp-config and --disable-slash-commands each remove only part of the startup work. Deleting project files is destructive and affects every user and tool, not just this script's runs.

questions.stem: A CI review job must use ONLY the MCP servers defined in a specific `--mcp-config` file and ignore any project- or user-level `.mcp.json`—but it still needs CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks to run normally. Which flag fits?

options.A: --bare, which starts a minimal session that ignores project- and user-level .mcp.json but also strips away the CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks this job still needs.
options.B: --strict-mcp-config, which uses only servers from the supplied --mcp-config and ignores other .mcp.json sources, leaving CLAUDE.md, skills, and hooks intact.
options.C: --disable-slash-commands, which turns off slash commands and skills so project- or user-level .mcp.json servers cannot be registered for the job.
options.D: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false, an environment variable that stops tool schemas from loading so only the supplied --mcp-config servers stay active.

questions.explanation: --strict-mcp-config scopes MCP configuration to just the supplied --mcp-config and ignores other .mcp.json sources, without touching the CLAUDE.md/skills/hooks this job still relies on. --bare would strip all of those away too, which the job needs. --disable-slash-commands governs skills/commands, not MCP config selection, and ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH controls tool-schema loading, not which servers load. This is the case where --bare is the wrong hammer.

questions.stem: You are about to run a new extraction prompt over 10,000 documents through the Message Batches API. How should you minimize the risk of a large-scale failure?

options.A: Submit all 10,000 immediately to get results as fast as possible.
options.B: Submit all 10,000 but wrap each request in a validation-and-retry loop for failures.
options.C: Test the prompt on a representative sample of 20–50 documents first, refine it, then submit the full batch.
options.D: Split into ten batches of 1,000 and submit them one after another.

questions.explanation: A flawed prompt applied to 10,000 documents produces 10,000 failures plus the cost of resubmitting them. Testing on a small representative sample surfaces prompt problems cheaply before committing to the full run. Submitting everything (with or without splitting/retry loops) still pays full price for a bad prompt; sequential 1,000-doc batches don't validate the prompt any earlier than a single sample would.

questions.stem: An automated code-review system flags issues but you cannot tell which rule triggered each finding, and you have no way to measure precision per rule. You want to make findings auditable and enable per-rule accuracy tracking. What should you add to the output?

options.A: A free-text field where the model writes out its reasoning and confidence level in prose for each individual finding it reports.
options.B: More severity levels—expand the three current tiers to ten so every finding is scored on a finer, more granular numeric scale.
options.C: Full model reasoning for every finding logged to a separate append-only file that reviewers can read through manually during later audits.
options.D: A structured detected_pattern field naming the specific rule that triggered each finding—an enum, plus a detail field for edge cases.

questions.explanation: A structured detected_pattern field attributes every finding to a specific rule, which makes each finding auditable and lets you compute precision per pattern and route findings by type. Free-text reasoning and separate reasoning logs are unstructured and not queryable at scale, and adding severity levels increases granularity without telling you which rule fired or how accurate each rule is.

questions.stem: A structured-extraction pipeline defines a single extraction tool with a strict JSON schema, but Claude intermittently responds with a conversational text answer instead of calling the tool. You have already added detailed instructions telling it to use the tool. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Change tool_choice from "auto" to "any" so a tool call is required rather than optional.
options.B: Add even more detailed natural-language instructions emphasizing that it must call the tool.
options.C: Add few-shot examples that always end in a tool call.
options.D: Add output validation that detects a plain-text response and automatically retries the request until a tool call comes back.

questions.explanation: With tool_choice: "auto" the model may still answer in text, so extra instructions, few-shot nudging, or catching-and-retrying the bad response only shift probabilities or add wasted round-trips—none make the tool call guaranteed. Switching to tool_choice: "any" (or forcing the single tool by name) makes a tool call mandatory, which is the deterministic guarantee the pipeline needs.

questions.stem: A customer is angry and rude in the chat, but their actual request is a standard product return that is clearly within the return policy, and the agent already has all the information needed to process it. The customer has not asked to speak with a human. What should the agent do?

options.A: Escalate to a human agent because the customer is visibly upset, treating negative sentiment as a reliable signal that the case needs human judgment.
options.B: Resolve the in-policy return autonomously since sentiment doesn't change complexity, offering a human only if the customer explicitly insists.
options.C: Ask a clarifying question first to de-escalate the customer's mood before acting on the return, since calming them improves the experience.
options.D: Process the return but also add a goodwill discount beyond policy to smooth things over and reduce the chance of an upset customer's negative review.

questions.explanation: Negative sentiment is not a reliable proxy for case difficulty—an angry customer with a routine, in-policy issue is exactly the kind of case the agent should handle end to end. Escalating on sentiment wastes human capacity and delays a resolution the agent could deliver now. The customer hasn't requested a human, so no clarifying-question-before-escalation nuance applies, and granting a discount beyond policy is an unauthorized decision, not a resolution.

questions.stem: A team wants black formatting applied to every Python file Claude Code edits, with a guarantee it happens on every edit rather than 'usually'. Which approach ensures it deterministically?

options.A: Add 'always run black after editing any .py file' to the project CLAUDE.md so the instruction is in context every session.
options.B: A PostToolUse hook matching Edit/Write on *.py that runs black on the changed file after the tool call completes.
options.C: Create a .claude/rules/ entry with a *.py glob instructing Claude to format edited Python with black.
options.D: Add a few-shot example to the system prompt showing an edit immediately followed by a black run.

questions.explanation: Anything the model reads—CLAUDE.md, a .claude/rules glob, or a few-shot example—only influences behavior probabilistically; the model can still skip the step. The only deterministic guarantee is code that runs outside the model: a PostToolUse hook fires on every matching Edit/Write regardless of what the model decides, so formatting always happens.

questions.stem: A compliance requirement states Claude Code must never write to files under /secrets, with no exceptions. What enforces this deterministically?

options.A: A bold 'NEVER write to /secrets' directive placed at the top of the project CLAUDE.md.
options.B: A .claude/rules/ file scoped to /secrets/** telling Claude to refuse any edit there.
options.C: A PreToolUse hook on Write/Edit that denies (blocks) any path under /secrets before the tool runs.
options.D: A user-level instruction in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md forbidding edits under /secrets.

questions.explanation: A hard 'no exceptions' guarantee cannot rest on instructions the model reads—CLAUDE.md text (project or user) and .claude/rules are all probabilistic and can be overridden or ignored. A PreToolUse hook evaluates the target path and blocks the call deterministically before it executes, which is the only option that actually enforces the rule.

questions.stem: A destructive delete_record tool must never execute without explicit human approval—a hard guarantee, not best-effort. What ensures it?

options.A: A PreToolUse hook on delete_record that blocks the call and requires an approval step before it can proceed.
options.B: A tool description stating 'only call this after the user has explicitly confirmed the deletion'.
options.C: A system-prompt rule instructing the model to always ask the user before deleting anything.
options.D: A few-shot example showing the model requesting confirmation before every deletion.

questions.explanation: The tool description, system-prompt rule, and few-shot example are all things the model reads, so they only make confirmation likely, not certain—the model can still call delete_record unprompted. A PreToolUse hook intercepts the call and gates it on approval outside the model, which is the deterministic guarantee the requirement demands.

questions.stem: In a multi-agent pipeline, a validation step must run after every subagent completes—the orchestrator can't rely on the model choosing to validate. What guarantees it runs every time?

options.A: Instruct the coordinator in its system prompt to always validate each subagent's output before continuing.
options.B: Add a CLAUDE.md note reminding the coordinator to validate after each subagent.
options.C: Give the coordinator a few-shot transcript that always validates before proceeding.
options.D: A PostToolUse hook on the Task tool that runs the validation step after each subagent call returns.

questions.explanation: Prompt instructions, CLAUDE.md reminders, and few-shot transcripts all influence the coordinator probabilistically—it may still continue without validating. A PostToolUse hook on Task fires deterministically after each subagent returns, so validation is guaranteed on every completion regardless of the model's choices.

questions.stem: A workflow requires that the test suite passes before Claude is allowed to mark a task complete, and this must hold every time. Which enforces it deterministically?

options.A: A CLAUDE.md instruction: 'never mark a task done until the tests pass'.
options.B: A Stop/PreToolUse hook that blocks completion unless the test command has exited 0.
options.C: A system-prompt line telling Claude to run the tests and only finish if they pass.
options.D: A .claude/rules/ entry requiring tests to pass before a task is completed.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md text, a system-prompt line, and .claude/rules are all read by the model and therefore probabilistic—Claude can still declare completion with failing or unrun tests. A hook that checks the test command's exit code and blocks completion enforces the gate in code outside the model, which is the only deterministic guarantee.

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline must guarantee the model's output is always valid JSON with a fixed set of fields—not merely 'usually parseable'. What guarantees the structure?

options.A: Define a tool_use input schema with the required fields so the API constrains output to that shape.
options.B: Add 'always respond in valid JSON with exactly these fields' to the prompt, with a formatting example.
options.C: Provide several few-shot examples of the exact JSON shape you want returned.
options.D: Instruct the model to double-check that its JSON is valid before responding.

questions.explanation: Prompt directives, few-shot examples, and self-check instructions only raise the odds of well-formed output—free-text generation can still drift or emit malformed JSON. A tool_use schema makes the model emit tool input that conforms to the declared structure, turning 'usually valid' into a structural guarantee (semantic correctness still needs separate validation).

questions.stem: An automated invoice-processing pipeline must extract fields into a JSON object that strictly conforms to a fixed schema; malformed or off-schema output breaks the downstream system with no human in the loop. A developer proposes prefilling the assistant response with `{` to force the model to emit JSON. What is the most reliable approach?

options.A: Prefill the assistant turn with `{` so the model must continue as JSON, then parse and forward the result.
options.B: Add an explicit "Respond with valid JSON only" instruction plus a few-shot example of the target object in the system prompt.
options.C: Define the object as a `tool_use` schema and set `tool_choice` to `"any"`, so the model must return a tool call matching the schema.
options.D: Prefill the assistant turn with the expected key skeleton (`{"invoice_id":`) and keep `tool_choice` at `"auto"`.

questions.explanation: Strict schema compliance for an unattended pipeline needs an enforced shape, which only `tool_use` with a JSON schema (forced via `tool_choice: "any"` or a named tool) provides. Prefilling (A, D) pins the opening tokens and can skip preamble, but it enforces no schema — the model can still drift off-shape, omit required fields, or emit invalid JSON after the prefilled prefix — and a prefill can't coexist with a forced tool call. Prompt-based instructions and few-shot (B) are followed inconsistently and can't be reliably parsed. Prefill and prompting steer output; only the schema guarantees it.

questions.stem: A conversational assistant returns correct summaries, but it keeps prepending a chatty preamble ("Sure! Here's the summary:") before the text. A downstream regex expects the response to begin immediately with the summary and breaks on the preamble. No structured schema is required — only the leading tokens must be controlled. What is the best fix?

options.A: Prefill the assistant turn with the opening of the summary so the model continues from there and never emits the preamble.
options.B: Switch the endpoint to `tool_use` with a single `summary` string field and `tool_choice: "any"` to force structured output.
options.C: Add a system-prompt instruction: "Do not include any preamble; begin your reply directly with the summary."
options.D: Set temperature to 0 so the model stops adding conversational filler.

questions.explanation: Controlling the first tokens / skipping preamble is exactly what response prefilling is for — begin the assistant turn with the summary's opening and the model continues in place, no preamble emitted. Forcing `tool_use` (B) is disproportionate: there's no schema to enforce, and wrapping a plain string in a tool adds machinery for a formatting nuisance. A prompt instruction (C) is followed inconsistently — the same class of failure. Temperature (D) controls randomness, not response structure. Prefill is the lightweight, reliable lever when the requirement is format/first-token control rather than schema compliance.

questions.stem: A team's root CLAUDE.md says "Never commit directly to `main`" and "Always run the linter before committing," but developers still occasionally push to `main` and skip the linter because Claude doesn't reliably follow the prose. How should they restructure the configuration?
