options.A: Move the two rules into a higher-in-the-hierarchy project CLAUDE.md and rephrase them emphatically (bold, "MUST").
options.B: Move the rules into a `.claude/rules/git.md` file loaded via a glob so they apply in every directory.
options.C: Duplicate the rules into both user-level and project-level CLAUDE.md so they always load no matter who clones the repo.
options.D: Add a pre-commit hook that blocks any commit to `main` and fails the commit if the linter does not pass.

questions.explanation: These are hard constraints that must hold regardless of model compliance, so they belong in an enforcement mechanism (a git/PreToolUse hook), not in prose. CLAUDE.md has no strict precedence and is always model-followed guidance — so re-scoping (A), moving to `.claude/rules/` (B), or duplicating across levels (C) all still depend on the model choosing to obey, which is the exact failure being reported. Guidance advises; hooks enforce.

questions.stem: A team needs three things configured for Claude Code: (1) the agent must be blocked from editing files under `infra/` without review; (2) Python docstring conventions should apply only when working inside `services/`; (3) a house preference — "prefer composition over inheritance" — that Claude should weigh but may override with a stated reason. Which configuration assigns each to the right mechanism?

options.A: All three in the root CLAUDE.md, with (1) written as "NEVER edit files under infra/."
options.B: (1) a settings.json permission deny (or PreToolUse hook); (2) a `.claude/rules/` file scoped by glob to `services/`; (3) a CLAUDE.md guideline.
options.C: (1) a CLAUDE.md rule; (2) a CLAUDE.md rule; (3) a PreToolUse hook that rejects any code using inheritance.
options.D: (1) `.claude/rules/infra.md`; (2) a settings.json permission; (3) `.claude/rules/style.md`.

questions.explanation: Match the mechanism to the guidance type. (1) is a hard constraint → deterministic enforcement (settings permission or PreToolUse hook). (2) is a convention that should load conditionally by path → `.claude/rules/` with a glob. (3) is a soft preference the model should apply with judgement → CLAUDE.md. A inverts this by leaving a hard block as prose; C both leaves the hard block as prose and puts a soft preference behind a hook (over-enforcing a judgement call); D uses path-scoped rules for a hard block and a permission for a formatting convention. Only B places enforce/scope/guide where each belongs.

questions.stem: A CLAUDE.md instructs the agent "Do not read files under `secrets/` or any `.env`." A security review finds the agent still reads them when a task appears to need config values. Which change most reliably prevents this?

options.A: Rewrite the instruction more forcefully and also add it to a `.claude/rules/security.md` loaded on every path.
options.B: Run the agent with `context: fork` so it works in an isolated context and can't reach the secrets.
options.C: Add a settings.json `deny` permission (or a PreToolUse hook) that blocks `Read` on `secrets/` and `.env`.
options.D: Add a PostToolUse hook that logs every read of `secrets/` or `.env` so the team can audit violations.

questions.explanation: The read must be prevented independent of model judgement, which only a deny permission or a PreToolUse gate on `Read` achieves. Strengthening the prose or adding a rules file (A) keeps it as model-followed guidance — the same thing that already failed. `context: fork` (B) isolates conversation context, not filesystem access, so it doesn't stop a Read. A PostToolUse log (D) is the tempting near-miss: it uses a hook, but it fires after the file has already been read — detection, not prevention — leaving the root problem (the access itself) unaddressed.

questions.stem: Your customer support agent runs on the Claude Agent SDK with max_turns set to 25 and a per-session max_budget_usd. A weekly audit finds that about 5% of sessions end with the customer neither helped nor handed to a human, and the ticket just stays open. Logs show that each of those sessions produced a final result message whose subtype was error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, or error_during_execution. Which change closes this gap?

options.A: In the orchestrator, read the subtype of each session's final result message and call escalate_to_human with a structured handoff whenever it is anything other than success.
options.B: Register a Stop hook that calls escalate_to_human whenever a session ends before the agent has called process_refund or recorded a resolution on the ticket.
options.C: Add a system-prompt rule that the agent must call escalate_to_human with a case summary whenever it cannot resolve the issue within its remaining turns.
options.D: Raise max_turns and max_budget_usd so that sessions have enough headroom to reach a resolution before either limit stops the agent loop.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The result message's subtype is the authoritative record of how the SDK loop ended. Only success carries `result`, and every error subtype still carries session_id, total_cost_usd, usage and num_turns. Orchestrator code that runs after every query() call can therefore build a handoff (or resume) for exactly the sessions that fell through. Wrapping the call in try/catch covers the one remaining exit path, a connection or process failure, which produces no result message. B fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 2, right mechanism family at the wrong point in the lifecycle): a hook looks deterministic, but the SDK docs warn that hooks may not fire when the agent hits the max_turns limit, and an API error ends the turn through StopFailure rather than Stop, so the hook misses the very sessions in the audit. C fails: a prompt rule is probabilistic, and the model never gets another turn to react when the budget cuts it off or execution errors out. D fails: raising the limits moves where sessions stop. Some still hit the limits, errors still happen, and runaway cost grows. What is missing is handling the exit, not avoiding it.

questions.stem: Your support agent's Messages API loop runs while stop_reason is "tool_use". It has a 15-iteration cap as a runaway backstop and retries failed API calls three times. Whenever the loop exits, for any reason, the orchestrator sends Claude's last text to the customer and closes the ticket as resolved. QA finds tickets closed as resolved where the customer got a half-finished reply or no reply at all. All of them come from sessions that hit the cap or ran out of API retries. What change fixes this?

options.A: Remove the iteration cap so the loop keeps running until Claude returns end_turn, and keep retrying failed API calls until one of them succeeds.
options.B: Close the ticket only when the loop exits on end_turn, and route exits caused by the cap or by exhausted retries to escalate_to_human with a handoff.
options.C: Before closing, ask Claude in one extra call whether the customer's issue was fully resolved, and close the ticket only when it answers yes.
options.D: Rerun the whole session from the start whenever it exits on the cap or on exhausted retries, and close the ticket once a rerun ends on end_turn.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The defect is that the orchestrator treats every loop exit as a resolution. Only an end_turn exit means Claude finished its answer. The cap firing and exhausted API retries are failure exits, so orchestrator code must route them to escalate_to_human with a structured handoff instead of closing the ticket; every session then ends in a resolution or an escalation. D fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 5, it patches the symptom instead of handling the exit): a rerun looks like a deterministic safeguard, but it is unbounded, a case that hit the cap or a persistent API outage will usually fail the same way again, and nothing in it ever hands the customer to a human. A fails: it blames the cap, but the cap is a legitimate secondary backstop behind stop_reason; removing it and retrying forever invites runaway loops and still gives persistent API errors no escalation path. C fails: a yes/no self-assessment is a self-reported signal, and a session that ended on API failure has no reliable model call left to ask.

questions.stem: A code-generation agent in your developer tooling writes files through a write_file tool whose input carries the complete file contents. The requests use max_tokens: 1024, a default copied from a chat feature, and for ordinary source files of a few hundred lines the API response comes back with stop_reason "max_tokens", and its last content block is a write_file tool_use whose input is cut off partway through the file. How should the agentic loop handle this response?

options.A: Execute write_file with the partial input that was received, append the tool_result, and let Claude correct the file on the next iteration.
options.B: Treat the response as the end of the task, the same as end_turn, and return the assistant's text so far to the developer as the result.
options.C: Discard the incomplete tool_use block and re-send the same request with a higher max_tokens value, then handle the new response.
options.D: Append a user message asking Claude to continue where it stopped, then join the new output onto the cut-off tool input and run it.

questions.explanation: C is correct. stop_reason "max_tokens" means the response was truncated. When the last block is an incomplete tool_use, the documented handling is to retry the request with a higher max_tokens to get the full tool call. Raising max_tokens is the right fix here because the truncation itself is the problem. D fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 2, right family but the wrong variant). Asking Claude to continue is a way to extend truncated text, but a tool_use input has to arrive as one complete block; splicing a continuation onto cut-off JSON is not the documented handling and risks an invalid call. A fails: running a tool on a partial input writes a truncated file, a real side effect produced by a malformed call. B fails: max_tokens is not end_turn. The task is unfinished and the text is not a final answer. The cap here is simply too low for a normal-sized file, which is why retrying with a higher max_tokens fits. If the output were inherently too large for one response (for example one change set for 40 modules, or findings for a 150-file review), raising the cap again would be the trap: split the work into smaller scoped calls and merge the results instead.

questions.stem: In the multi-agent research system, the web search subagent's API response ends with stop_reason "tool_use" and contains three tool_use blocks: search_papers, search_news, and fetch_patent. Your code runs them concurrently. The first two return results, but fetch_patent times out even after retries. How should the loop return the tool results before the next API call?

options.A: Send each tool_result in its own user message, one API call per result, in the order in which the three tools finish executing.
options.B: Return tool_results for search_papers and search_news only, and leave out fetch_patent so the model is not misled by the failed call.
options.C: Merge the three outputs into one plain-text block in the next user message, with a closing line noting that fetch_patent timed out.
options.D: Send one user message holding a tool_result for each of the three tool_use ids, with the fetch_patent result marked is_error: true.

questions.explanation: D is correct. For parallel calls, the loop returns one tool_result for each tool_use block, all together in the next user message, matched by tool_use_id and placed before any text. A call that failed or was not run still gets a tool_result with is_error: true and a brief explanation. The model then knows fetch_patent failed and can decide whether to retry, work around it, or report the gap. B fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 2, one result short of the exact protocol): leaving out a result leaves a tool_use id unanswered, and it hides an access failure that the model and the coordinator need to reason about. A fails: parallel results belong together in the next single user message, not spread across separate messages and API calls. C fails: results must be tool_result blocks tied to their tool_use_id, and a merged plain-text summary loses that link.

questions.stem: In a customer support system, an intake agent verifies the caller with get_customer, and a supervisor then approves a refund of up to $150 for one specific order. A separate refund agent, started in a fresh session and configured with a standard $500 refund limit, executes the refund. Audits show the refund agent sometimes asks the customer to verify again, and twice it refunded more than the approved amount. The refund must never run for an unverified customer or above the approved cap. What should the architect implement?

options.A: Resume the intake agent's session inside the refund step so the verification result and the supervisor's approval already in the conversation carry over to it.
options.B: Have the intake step emit a handoff record with the verified customer ID, how it was verified, the approver, cap and order ID, and gate process_refund on those fields.
options.C: Append the full intake transcript, including every tool result and the supervisor's approval message, to the refund agent's prompt with an instruction to honor the approval.
options.D: Add a gate in the refund agent that blocks process_refund until its own get_customer call returns a verified ID and the amount is within its standard $500 limit.

questions.explanation: B is correct. It makes the authorization state an explicit structured artifact: who was verified, by which tool, who approved, the cap, and the order it applies to. A prerequisite gate on process_refund checks those exact fields before the call runs, so every refund is blocked unless the customer is verified and the amount is within the $150 approved for that order. The refund agent gets the verified state, so it has no reason to re-verify. D is the strongest near-miss: it is also a deterministic gate, and it does guarantee a verified customer, but it checks the wrong limit. The agent's generic $500 limit still allows the over-cap refunds that were reported, and gating on its own get_customer call makes the re-verification the stem complains about mandatory. A resumes the conversation, not an enforced state: the approval exists only as prose the refund agent has to interpret, and nothing stops it from exceeding the cap. C carries the same information but buries it in a transcript, and honoring the cap still depends on the model following an instruction, which has a non-zero failure rate.

questions.stem: A support agent handles a dispute over a $300 duplicate charge. It verified the customer through get_customer and applied a $40 account credit, the most it may issue without approval, then escalates the remaining $260 to a tier-2 human who works in a separate console with no access to the conversation transcript. Tier-2 staff report that they often re-run identity checks the agent already completed, and in several cases refunded the full $300 on top of the credit. What should the escalation payload contain?

options.A: Labeled fields for the customer ID, the root-cause diagnosis, the $300 duplicate charge as the refund amount, and a recommended next action for tier-2 to take.
options.B: The full conversation transcript with every tool result attached as a file, plus the customer ID in the ticket header so tier-2 can locate the account quickly.
options.C: Labeled fields for the customer ID verified via get_customer, the root cause, the $40 credit already applied, the $260 still owed, and a recommended next action.
options.D: The customer ID, root cause and recommended action, plus an instruction for tier-2 to re-verify identity and look up any credits on the account before refunding.

questions.explanation: C is correct. It keeps the core handoff fields and adds the authorization state the reported failures need: that identity was already verified and how, that the $40 credit was already applied, and that only $260 is still owed. With that, tier-2 neither repeats the identity check nor refunds the full $300 on top of the credit. A is the strongest near-miss. It has the right structure, labeled fields, but it treats a neighbouring problem (missing case context) and not the stated one (lost verification and completed-action state). Tier-2 still can't tell the customer was verified, and the $300 refund amount ignores the credit, which is exactly how the double refunds happen. B hands over raw material instead of a compiled summary: tier-2 has to re-derive what was verified and done from the transcript, which is the re-work a structured handoff exists to prevent. D makes the redundant re-verification a rule and still leaves the applied credit and the outstanding amount out of the payload.

questions.stem: A developer runs `claude mcp add --transport http tracker https://tracker.example.com/mcp` and sees the `Added …` confirmation line. In a new session, asked to summarize ticket PROJ-42, Claude searches the repository with Grep instead, and when asked which tools it has for tickets it names only built-in tools. A teammate says the tracker tools' descriptions are too sparse, so Claude prefers built-ins. What should the developer do first?

options.A: Rewrite the tracker tools' descriptions to explain their capabilities and outputs in detail so that Claude prefers them over Grep for ticket lookups.
options.B: Re-add the server with `claude mcp add --scope project` so the configuration is committed to `.mcp.json` and loaded in every developer session.
options.C: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to always use the tracker MCP tools, never Grep or Bash, whenever a ticket ID is mentioned.
options.D: Run `claude mcp list`, or open `/mcp` inside the session, and check the tracker server's connection status and how many tools it exposes.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The `Added …` line only means the configuration was written; `claude mcp add` does not validate that the server connects. `claude mcp list` shows each server's health (Connected, Needs authentication, Failed to connect, Pending approval), and `/mcp` shows the same status plus the tool count and lets you sign in with OAuth. Claude naming only built-in tools points at discovery, not selection, so confirm the server connected before changing anything else. A is the strongest near-miss because enriching descriptions is a real Guide 2.4 fix for when Claude prefers built-ins over capable MCP tools. It fixes a neighbouring problem, though: choosing among tools that are present. If the server never connected, there are no tracker descriptions in play to improve. B changes who shares the config, not whether the server connects, and it commits an unverified server to the team. C only influences selection and has the same flaw as A: it assumes the tools exist.

questions.stem: A team commits a `.mcp.json` that configures a remote issue-tracker server named `tracker` with `"headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}"}`. A new developer clones the repository, approves the project server, and starts Claude Code. `claude mcp list` shows a missing-variable warning naming TRACKER_TOKEN, and the server fails to connect with a 401. The team wants every developer on the same shared server definition, with no credentials in version control. What should the new developer do?

options.A: Export their own TRACKER_TOKEN in the shell that launches Claude Code, restart it, and check the server's status again in `claude mcp list`.
options.B: Replace `${TRACKER_TOKEN}` in `.mcp.json` with their personal token, then add `.mcp.json` to `.gitignore` so the edited copy is never committed.
options.C: Change the header in `.mcp.json` to `Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN:-<team service token>}` so developers without the variable fall back to one shared token.
options.D: Add a server with the same name via `claude mcp add --scope user`, putting their personal token directly in the header of that entry in `~/.claude.json`.

questions.explanation: A is correct. An unset `${VAR}` with no default does not stop the server from loading. Claude Code loads it with the literal `${TRACKER_TOKEN}` text and shows a missing-variable warning in `claude mcp list` and `/mcp`, so the tracker receives `Bearer ${TRACKER_TOKEN}` and rejects it. Setting the variable in the developer's own environment makes the committed definition expand correctly, which keeps the team on one definition and the secret out of git. D is the strongest near-miss: keeping a personal credential in personal config sounds right, but it creates a second, forked definition of a server the team wants shared. It also does not take effect: when the same server name is defined in more than one scope the order is local > project > user and the whole entry from the winning scope is used, with no field merging, so the project `.mcp.json` entry still wins and the user copy is shadowed. B edits the shared file and relies on `.gitignore`, which does not untrack a file already committed, so the token is one commit away from leaking. C commits a real secret as the default value.

questions.stem: A platform team's committed root CLAUDE.md mixes two kinds of lines. Some are hard prohibitions: "Never edit anything under `db/migrations/`" and "Never read `.env` files." Others are style guidance: "Prefer early returns" and "Name booleans with an is/has prefix." A security review finds that Claude Code edited a migration during refactors on two developers' machines. The team wants the prohibitions to hold for everyone who clones the repository, and wants the style guidance to stay advice that Claude can weigh against the situation. How should they restructure the configuration?

options.A: Move the two prohibitions into `.claude/rules/security.md` with `paths: ["db/migrations/**", "**/.env"]`, and keep the style guidance in CLAUDE.md.
options.B: Add `Edit(db/migrations/**)` and `Read(**/.env)` to `permissions.deny` in each developer's `.claude/settings.local.json`, and move the style guidance into `.claude/rules/style.md`.
options.C: Add `Edit(db/migrations/**)` and `Read(**/.env)` to `permissions.deny` in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, and keep the style guidance in CLAUDE.md.
options.D: Add `Edit(db/migrations/**)` and `Read(**/.env)` to `permissions.deny` in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, and add a PreToolUse hook that rejects edits without early returns.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. The memory docs say Claude treats CLAUDE.md as "context, not enforced configuration", and the permissions docs say CLAUDE.md shapes "what Claude tries to do, but they don't change what Claude Code allows". Claude Code enforces permission rules itself. The committed `.claude/settings.json` is the shared project scope, so every clone gets the deny rules. The style lines stay in CLAUDE.md as behavioural guidance.
B is the strongest near-miss: right mechanism, wrong file. `.claude/settings.local.json` is personal, so a new clone gets no deny and the team depends on every developer remembering to add it. (Moving the style lines into a rules file would be harmless; the scope is what fails.)
A only moves the text. A `paths`-scoped rule loads when Claude works with matching files, but it is still context the model can ignore, which is the same failure that already happened.
D enforces the prohibitions correctly but also puts a style preference behind a blocking hook. The team said that preference should stay advice, and such a hook would reject reasonable edits.

questions.stem: A team's committed `.claude/settings.json` contains `"deny": ["Bash(curl *)"]` to stop Claude Code from sending data to arbitrary hosts. A new health-check workflow needs Claude to run curl against `https://status.internal.example.com`. A developer added `Bash(curl https://status.internal.example.com/*)` to the `allow` list in their `.claude/settings.local.json`, but Claude Code still blocks the call. The team lead agrees to change the shared configuration. Which change lets Claude reach that one host while every other curl call stays blocked?

options.A: Move the narrow allow rule from `.claude/settings.local.json` into the committed `.claude/settings.json`, next to the curl deny.
options.B: Launch Claude Code with `--allowedTools "Bash(curl https://status.internal.example.com/*)"` for the health-check sessions.
options.C: Keep the curl deny and add a PreToolUse hook that returns an allow decision for curl commands whose URL is on that host.
options.D: Replace the curl deny with a PreToolUse hook that inspects each curl command and blocks any whose URL is not on that host.

questions.explanation:
D is correct. The permissions docs say rules are evaluated "deny, then ask, then allow", that the first match decides, and that "rule specificity doesn't change the order". They also say "An allow rule can't carve an exception out of a deny rule." So as long as `Bash(curl *)` is denied, no allow rule for curl can take effect. The docs list a PreToolUse hook that "validates URLs in Bash commands and blocks disallowed domains" as a way to filter URLs, and "A blocking hook also takes precedence over allow rules." Once the broad deny is gone, the developer's narrow allow can apply to the one host, and the hook blocks every other host.
C is the strongest near-miss: the right tool used the wrong way. "Hook decisions don't bypass permission rules", so the matching deny still blocks the call when the hook returns allow.
A misreads the problem as a scope mismatch. Deny rules are evaluated before allow rules whatever file they are in, so an allow in the same file still loses.
B misreads it as a precedence problem. "If a tool is denied at any level, no other level can allow it", and command-line arguments don't change that.

questions.stem: A monorepo team moved its Terraform conventions out of the root CLAUDE.md into `.claude/rules/terraform.md` to stop them using tokens in frontend sessions. Terraform files live in `infra/`, `modules/`, and `services/*/deploy/`. A week later the team finds the Terraform conventions still in context at the start of every session, including sessions that never touch a `.tf` file. The rule file opens with a `# Terraform conventions` heading, followed by the bullet list. What change makes the conventions load only when Claude works with Terraform files?

options.A: Add YAML frontmatter to `terraform.md` with `paths: ["**/*.tf", "**/*.tfvars"]`.
options.B: Move the conventions into `infra/CLAUDE.md` so they load when Claude works inside that directory.
options.C: Turn `terraform.md` into a skill at `.claude/skills/terraform/SKILL.md` that developers invoke before Terraform work.
options.D: Delete the rule file and pull the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md with an `@docs/terraform.md` import.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. The memory docs say rules without `paths` frontmatter "are loaded at launch with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`". The file starts straight with a heading, so it has no frontmatter, and moving text into `.claude/rules/` does not make it conditional by itself. A `paths` glob does: the rule loads only when Claude works with matching files, and a `**/*.tf` glob matches Terraform files in every directory.
D is the strongest near-miss. It solves a neighbouring problem, organisation, rather than the stated one, conditional loading. Imported files "are expanded and loaded into context at launch", so the conventions would still be in every session.
B covers only `infra/` and misses `modules/` and `services/*/deploy/`. This is the Guide's point that glob rules beat directory CLAUDE.md files when files are spread across the codebase.
C makes the conventions depend on someone remembering to invoke a skill. The team wants them applied automatically whenever Claude works on Terraform files.

questions.stem: A platform team is configuring Claude Code for a monorepo and has three pieces of guidance: (1) a 120-line release checklist whose full text should enter context only when someone is cutting a release; (2) GraphQL resolver conventions that should load automatically whenever Claude works on resolver files, which sit in `resolvers/` folders across a dozen packages, and should stay out of context during other work; (3) a requirement that `make stubs` regenerates the client stubs every time Claude changes a `.proto` file, with no exceptions. Which configuration fits each piece?

options.A: (1) `.claude/rules/release.md` with no `paths` field; (2) `.claude/rules/resolvers.md` with `paths: ["**/resolvers/*.ts"]`; (3) a PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write for `*.proto` that runs `make stubs`.
options.B: (1) a skill in `.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md`; (2) `.claude/rules/resolvers.md` with `paths: ["**/resolvers/*.ts"]`; (3) a PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write for `*.proto` that runs `make stubs`.
options.C: (1) a skill in `.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md`; (2) `.claude/rules/resolvers.md` with `paths: ["**/resolvers/*.ts"]`; (3) a PreToolUse hook on Edit|Write for `*.proto` that runs `make stubs`.
options.D: (1) `.claude/rules/release.md` with no `paths` field; (2) a resolver section in the root CLAUDE.md; (3) `.claude/rules/proto.md` with `paths: ["**/*.proto"]` telling Claude to run `make stubs`.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. Each piece goes to the mechanism that matches when it applies. (1) Only for one task → a skill: its description is in context from the start, and its full content loads only when it is invoked. (2) Whenever Claude works with matching files, across many folders, and not otherwise → a `.claude/rules/` file with a `paths` glob. (3) On every matching edit, with no exceptions → a hook. It must be PostToolUse, because it has to run after the `.proto` change is written.
C is the strongest near-miss: the right mechanism on the wrong event. PreToolUse runs before the edit, so `make stubs` would regenerate from the old `.proto` file.
A misses on one piece: a rules file with no `paths` field loads at launch in every session, so the 120-line checklist would sit in context during unrelated work.
D fails all three. The checklist rule and the root CLAUDE.md section both load in every session. The stub regeneration becomes a rule the model reads, which can load correctly and still be skipped, and that fails "with no exceptions".

questions.stem: A developer on a Developer Productivity team asks Claude Code to simplify the `calculateTax` function in `src/billing/invoice.ts` for a one-time cleanup ticket. No teammate needs this file for their own work, and later sessions will not need it either. What is the most effective way to give Claude this file as context?

options.A: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md stating that the tax logic lives in `src/billing/invoice.ts`, then ask for the refactor.
options.B: Describe the file's location in the prompt ("the invoice module in the billing folder") and let Claude search for it.
options.C: Add `@src/billing/invoice.ts` as an import in the project CLAUDE.md, then ask for the refactor in the prompt.
options.D: Reference `@src/billing/invoice.ts` in the prompt itself, in the same message that asks Claude to simplify `calculateTax`.

questions.explanation: D is correct: an `@file` reference in a prompt includes the full content of that file in the conversation. That fits the need exactly: one file, one task, no later sessions. C is the near-miss: the `@` syntax is right, but an `@import` in CLAUDE.md is expanded at launch in every session, and a project CLAUDE.md reaches every teammate. Imports help organisation but do not reduce context, so this is far too heavy for a one-off. A is also persistent and team-wide for a one-time need, and it only tells Claude where to look instead of giving it the content. B goes against the documented best practice to reference files with @ instead of describing where code lives: Claude has to search first and may land on the wrong file.

questions.stem: In a Code Generation session, a developer types: `@src/payments/ compare the retry logic in client.ts and webhook.ts and unify it`. Claude starts its reply by reading the two files. A teammate watching says those reads were wasted, because `@src/payments/` had already put every file in the folder into the conversation. What does the directory reference actually provide, and how should the developer write the prompt next time?

options.A: A listing of the folder's files, not their contents; reference `@src/payments/client.ts` and `@src/payments/webhook.ts`.
options.B: The folder's `CLAUDE.md` file only; move the retry conventions into `src/payments/CLAUDE.md` so they load with the reference.
options.C: The full contents of every file, trimmed at the context limit; split the request into one prompt per file to stay under it.
options.D: The full contents of every file in the folder; the extra reads are redundant, so tell Claude to skip re-reading those files.

questions.explanation: A is correct: a directory reference shows file listings, not contents. To put the contents in the conversation, reference each file with `@path`; a single message can reference several files. D is the near-miss and the teammate's claim: it is the right mechanism family (`@` references) but assumes a directory reference behaves like a file reference. The reads were not redundant, and telling Claude to skip them would leave it working from file names alone. B misapplies a real fact: an `@` FILE reference also adds the CLAUDE.md files of that file's directory and its parents, but the docs do not say a directory reference provides a CLAUDE.md, let alone only that. It also turns a code-comparison task into a conventions problem. C invents truncation behaviour, and splitting the request per file would break the comparison the developer asked for.

questions.stem: A CI/CD engineer asks Claude Code to add a NOT NULL `region` column to the `orders` table. The code change is a single new migration file, but Claude will apply it by running `npm run migrate` through Bash against the shared staging database, and the migration backfills and rewrites existing rows that other teams rely on. The engineer says: "It's one file, so just run it, and if it's wrong we'll rewind." What approach should they take?

options.A: Use direct execution to write and run the migration, then use `/rewind` to restore the earlier checkpoint if the backfill is wrong.
options.B: Use plan mode to inspect the schema and draft the migration, have the plan reviewed, then approve running it against staging.
options.C: Use direct execution after an Explore subagent summarises the `orders` schema, then write and run the migration in one step.
options.D: Use direct execution, but commit the working tree to git before running the migration so the change can be reverted if needed.

questions.explanation: B is correct: the diff is small, but its effect is not something a rewind can undo. Checkpoints track only edits made through Claude's file-editing tools; changes made through Bash commands or external processes are not captured, and checkpoints are not a replacement for git. The staging rows the backfill rewrites are not a tracked file at all. So the migration should be planned and reviewed before it runs, and in plan mode Claude reads the schema and writes the plan but makes no edits until the plan is approved. A is the near-miss: it solves a neighbouring problem, undoing Claude's own file edits. `/rewind` could remove the migration file, not the rows the migration already rewrote. D has the same flaw: git can revert the migration file, not the data. C adds discovery but still runs the migration with no plan or review first; the risk was never missing context about the schema.

questions.stem: A team must change how the API gateway and three backend services refresh authentication tokens. The security team and the tech lead have asked to approve the approach before any code is written. A developer will do the work in Claude Code. Which workflow fits this requirement?

options.A: Use direct execution on a feature branch and open a draft pull request so the security team and tech lead review the diff.
options.B: Use direct execution with upfront instructions that restate the approach the tech lead outlined in the team's chat thread.
options.C: Use plan mode to produce the plan, send it to the security team and tech lead, and implement only after they accept it.
options.D: Use plan mode to explore the four services, then approve the plan yourself and switch to direct execution to implement it.

questions.explanation: C is correct: the requirement is approval of the approach before implementation. In plan mode Claude explores the code and writes a plan without editing source until the plan is approved, so the plan can go to the security team and tech lead first and the edits start only after they accept it. The work also spans four services and is security-sensitive, which the Guide assigns to plan mode. D is the near-miss: plan-then-execute is the right shape (the same hybrid the Guide recommends for a library migration), but the developer approves their own plan, so the people the stem names never see it before code is written. A provides a review, but of finished code after implementation; any rejected approach means rework. B assumes the approach is already settled by an informal chat, so there is no reviewed artefact and no exploration of the four services before coding.

questions.stem: A code-migration agent in your developer tooling applies its work through an apply_changes tool whose input is a single change set holding the full rewritten contents of every module it touched. For a migration covering 40 service modules, the API response comes back with stop_reason "max_tokens", and its last content block is an apply_changes tool_use whose input is cut off partway through a module. The team has already raised max_tokens twice. Each raise gets the change set a few modules further before it is cut off, and the migration list grows every sprint. What should the team change?

options.A: Execute apply_changes with the partial input that was received, append the tool_result, and let Claude rewrite the remaining modules next turn.
options.B: Discard the incomplete tool_use block, request the change set for a few modules per API call, and merge the change sets before applying them.
options.C: Discard the incomplete tool_use block and re-send the same request with max_tokens raised to the model's maximum output limit.
options.D: Append a user message asking Claude to continue where it stopped, join the new output onto the cut-off tool input, and then run it.

questions.explanation: B is correct. stop_reason "max_tokens" means the response was cut off, so the partial apply_changes call is discarded and never run. The stem shows the output is inherently too large for one response: each raise only gets a few modules further, and the change set grows with every module added. The fix is to make each call smaller, asking for the change set of a few modules per call, and to merge the complete change sets in code before applying them, so the migration still lands as one unit. C is the strongest near-miss (axis 5, it patches the symptom). Retrying an incomplete tool_use with a higher max_tokens is the documented move when the cap was set too low for a normal-sized answer. Here, though, every model has a fixed maximum output, very large max_tokens values need streaming to avoid dropped connections, and the growing migration list will pass any ceiling. A fails: running the tool on a cut-off input writes a broken module, a real side effect from a malformed call. D fails: a tool_use input must arrive as one complete block, and joining a continuation onto cut-off JSON can repeat or skip content, with no guarantee the result still matches the tool schema.

questions.stem: Your Structured Data Extraction pipeline sends each supplier price catalogue to Claude with an extract_line_items tool whose input schema is an array of line items (sku, description, unit_price, currency, and an optional discount). Most catalogues work. The largest ones, around 400 pages and 6,000 items across 35 product sections, fit easily in the context window, but they return a tool_use cut off mid-array with stop_reason "max_tokens", even though max_tokens is already set high. Supplier catalogues grow every season, and downstream validation rejects these extractions. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Raise max_tokens to the model's maximum output limit and keep sending each catalogue as one extraction request.
options.B: Move the pipeline to a model with a larger context window so each catalogue and its extraction fit in one request.
options.C: Remove the optional fields from the line-item schema so each item uses fewer tokens and the whole array fits in one response.
options.D: Send each product section as its own extract_line_items request with the same schema, then merge the item arrays in code.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The catalogue fits the context window. What fails is the output: a line-item array that grows with the catalogue and is cut off with stop_reason "max_tokens". Sending one request per product section with the same schema returns 35 complete, schema-valid arrays, and code merges them into one extraction (and can check that every section returned a result). A is the strongest near-miss (axis 5, it patches the symptom). Raising max_tokens is the reflex for truncation, but it is already set high, each model has a fixed maximum output, and a 6,000-item array that grows every season will pass any ceiling. B is a neighbouring diagnosis: a bigger context window helps an input that does not fit, but this input already fits, and the context window and the maximum output are separate limits. C throws away data the schema was designed to capture (a discount printed in the catalogue now has nowhere to go) and only postpones the ceiling until a larger catalogue arrives.

questions.stem: In your CI/CD pipeline, a nightly job audits every file changed on the release branch, often 150 or more files. It calls the Messages API with a report_findings tool whose input is one array of findings, and each finding concerns a single file. On large releases the tool_use is cut off with stop_reason "max_tokens", the job cannot parse the findings, and nothing gets posted. What should the team do so the audit reliably reports on every file?

options.A: Call the API once per batch of about ten changed files with the same report_findings tool, then merge the findings arrays in code.
options.B: Raise max_tokens to the model's maximum output limit for the audit job and fail it only when a response is still cut off.
options.C: Instruct the model to keep each finding's description under twenty words so the findings for all files fit in one response.
options.D: Stream the response and post every finding that arrived complete before the stream stopped with stop_reason max_tokens.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Each finding concerns a single file, so the audit splits cleanly: one call per batch of about ten files returns a complete, schema-valid findings array, and code merges the arrays into one report before posting. The output of each call stays within what one response can hold, however large the release gets. B is the strongest near-miss (axis 5, it patches the symptom). A higher max_tokens only moves the cut-off point: every model has a fixed maximum output, very large values need streaming for long requests, and the next larger release fails again. C shrinks each finding, which strips the detail developers need to act on and still leaves the total output growing with the file count. D keeps the findings that arrived before the cut-off and silently drops every file after it, so the job reports a partial audit as complete.

questions.stem: Your team's custom review agent, built on the Claude API, already checks every pull request for style violations and common security issues. The team adds a second review stage that runs Claude Code in GitHub Actions. This stage keeps reporting the same style and security findings the first agent already covers. The team decides that in this repository style and security belong to that dedicated agent, so every Claude Code review of the repository should skip those categories and report only other defects. What should they do?

options.A: Add an exclusion list of the style and security rules as a custom input to the Claude Code step in the GitHub Actions workflow file.
options.B: Store the excluded rule categories in a GitHub Actions environment variable that the review job reads before Claude runs.
options.C: Document in the repository's CLAUDE.md that the dedicated agent covers style and security, which reviews must skip, and what they should report.
options.D: Add a GitHub Actions job after the review that removes findings matching the first agent's categories before they are posted.

questions.explanation:
C is correct. CLAUDE.md is the documented place for review criteria and project-specific rules, and Claude Code reads it on every run. Writing down which categories the first agent covers (and must be skipped) and what this stage should report changes what the model itself treats as a finding, so the fix sits at the cause.
D is the strongest near-miss. A filter job after the review is deterministic, but it acts only after the model has already spent turns on the excluded categories. It also depends on the model labelling each finding's category the same way on every run: a mislabelled real defect gets deleted, and a mislabelled style nit slips through. The review itself is unchanged, so it patches the symptom.
A fails because the action reads only the inputs it defines (prompt, claude_args, settings and so on), and none of them excludes review categories. An extra custom input never becomes text Claude reads, so its judgement stays the same.
B fails because an environment variable belongs to the process, not to the model's context. Nothing in Claude's prompt or CLAUDE.md mentions it, and in the action's automation mode Claude has no shell access to read it unless someone grants one.
Why CLAUDE.md and not --append-system-prompt: the rule here applies to every Claude Code review of the repository, so it belongs in the project CLAUDE.md that every run reads. A rule meant for one specific invocation only, without changing other sessions, would go in --append-system-prompt for that run (see q227).

questions.stem: Your GitHub Actions workflow runs `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` with a plain-text review `prompt` on every pull request, and Claude posts its findings as inline comments. To stop runs from stalling, a developer set `claude_args: '--allowedTools "Bash,Edit,mcp__github_inline_comment__create_inline_comment"'`. A security audit then found review runs in which Claude ran `curl` and `npm install` and edited files in the checkout, although the review only needs to read the code and post inline comments. The team wants review runs to be unable to do anything beyond that. What should they change?

options.A: Change `claude_args` to `--allowedTools "mcp__github_inline_comment__create_inline_comment"`, removing `Bash` and `Edit` from the granted tools.
options.B: Add a rule to the repository's CLAUDE.md stating that review runs must never run shell commands or edit files in the checkout.
options.C: Change the job's GitHub `permissions` block from `contents: write` to `contents: read` for the review job.
options.D: Add a workflow step after the review that runs `git checkout -- .` to discard any file changes left on the runner.

questions.explanation:
A is correct. In the action's automation mode Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until tools are granted with `--allowedTools` in `claude_args`, so the grant list is the review's access boundary. Removing `Bash` and `Edit` takes away the ability to run `curl`/`npm install` and to edit files. Read-only tools such as Read, Grep and Glob need no grant, so the review can still read the code, and the inline-comment tool stays granted (the action starts that MCP server only when `--allowedTools` names it).
B is the strongest near-miss. CLAUDE.md is the right home for review standards, but a line in it is text the model reads: it makes shell use less likely, while `Bash` and `Edit` remain granted, so nothing makes the runs unable to use them. The stem asks for a guarantee.
C treats a neighbouring problem. The `permissions` block scopes the workflow's GitHub token, meaning what the job may write back to the repository. It does not change which tools Claude may run on the runner, so the `curl` calls and file edits still happen.
D patches the symptom after the fact. By the time the cleanup step runs, the shell commands have already executed (with network access and possibly secrets in the environment), and discarding edits afterwards does not restrict anything.

questions.stem: Your CI review sends each pull request to Claude with one prompt that checks security, business-logic correctness, and API-design consistency, with few-shot examples for each. After the team added six new security examples to reduce missed injection flaws, security recall improved, but API-design findings such as breaking changes to public endpoints and inconsistent error shapes dropped sharply on the same evaluation set. Pull request sizes did not change. What should the team do?

options.A: Add six new API-design examples to the same prompt, matching the number of security examples it now contains.
options.B: Add a verification pass after the review that re-checks each reported finding against the diff and drops any it cannot confirm.
options.C: Move the review to a higher-tier model with a larger context window that can hold every concern's examples in one prompt.
options.D: Run separate security, business-logic, and API-design passes over the pull request, each with its own prompt and few-shot examples.

questions.explanation:
D is correct. The security, business-logic and API-design concerns compete inside one prompt, so strengthening one (six new security examples) pulls recall away from another. Separate passes, each with its own prompt and its own few-shot examples, let each concern be tuned without moving the others. The merged findings still cover all three.
A is the strongest near-miss. Balancing the example counts keeps every concern in the same prompt, so the competition remains. The prompt keeps growing, and the next round of tuning shifts recall again. It patches the symptom.
B treats a neighbouring problem. A verification pass improves precision by removing wrong findings from what was reported. The problem here is recall: API-design issues the combined prompt never reported are not in the list, so there is nothing for the verifier to confirm.
C adds capacity the prompt does not lack, since it already fits and pull request sizes did not change. A larger context window does not stop the concerns from trading recall.

questions.stem: A payments team is designing an automated pull request review. Three groups want findings: the security team (injection, missing authorization checks), the product team (violations of refund and discount rules), and the platform team (breaking changes to public API contracts). Most pull requests touch two to four files. In a prototype that used one combined prompt, every time one group's few-shot examples were tuned, recall for the other groups' categories fell. Which review architecture should they build?

options.A: Review each changed file in its own pass with the combined prompt, then run one integration pass across files for cross-file data flow.
options.B: Run one pass per concern (security, business rules, API contracts), each with its own prompt and few-shot examples, then merge the findings.
options.C: Keep the combined prompt and add an instruction telling Claude to give the three concerns equal attention on every pull request.
options.D: Run the combined prompt three times on each pull request and report only the findings that appear in at least two of the three runs.

questions.explanation:
B is correct. The prototype shows a recall trade-off between concerns: tuning one group's examples lowers the other groups' recall. So each concern gets its own pass with its own prompt and few-shot examples, and the findings are merged into one report. Each team's pass can then be tuned without moving the others.
A is the strongest near-miss. Per-file passes plus an integration pass are the right fix for attention dilution across many files, but these pull requests touch only two to four files, and every file pass would still run the combined prompt, so the concerns keep competing. It treats a neighbouring problem.
C keeps all concerns in one prompt and relies on an instruction to give them equal attention, which does not remove the competition the prototype measured.
D, consensus over three runs of the same combined prompt, keeps the same blind spots in every run and suppresses real findings that are only caught some of the time.

questions.stem: A team runs Claude Code with `claude -p` in a GitHub Actions job to review every pull request. The team's review criteria (for example, every new endpoint must call `authorize()`, and controllers must not build raw SQL) were written by the tech lead in her `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. When she runs the review command on her laptop, violations of these criteria are flagged; in the CI job, the same violations pass without comment. The team wants every CI run and every developer's local review to apply the same criteria. What should they do?

options.A: Add a workflow step that copies the tech lead's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the runner's home directory before the review runs.
options.B: Add `--bare` to the `claude -p` review command in the CI job, keeping the rest of the workflow unchanged.
options.C: Add `--append-system-prompt "Apply the team's review criteria"` to the `claude -p` review command in the CI job.
options.D: Move the review criteria from the tech lead's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the repository's committed `CLAUDE.md` file.

questions.explanation: D is correct. A CI runner checks out only committed files, and a `claude -p` run loads the project `CLAUDE.md` from the checkout plus whatever sits in the runner's own `~/.claude`, which is normally nothing. The memory docs scope `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` to "Just you (all projects)" and the project `CLAUDE.md` to "Team members via source control". The GitHub Actions docs say to define review criteria and project rules in the repository's `CLAUDE.md`. Moving the criteria there gives CI and every developer the same rules, versioned with the code. A is the strongest near-miss. Copying her file onto the runner does make CI flag the violations, but it only patches the symptom: the team's rules still live in one person's private, unversioned file, other developers still don't get them, and her personal preferences leak into every CI review. B makes things worse, because `--bare` skips auto-discovery of every `CLAUDE.md`, including the project one. C adds a sentence that names "the team's review criteria" but carries none of their content, so Claude still doesn't know them.

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions job runs `claude -p "Review this PR and report issues" --dangerously-skip-permissions --output-format json --json-schema "$(cat review-schema.json)"`, and a later step posts each finding from `structured_output` as an inline PR comment. A developer added `--dangerously-skip-permissions` after early runs had tool calls denied. Since then, some runs have edited source files to "fix" the issues they found, and one run executed `npm install` and a project script. The review must still read the code and the diff, but it must not modify files, install packages, or execute project scripts. What should the team change?

options.A: Add "Only read code and report findings; never edit files or run commands" to the review prompt passed to `claude -p`.
options.B: Replace `--dangerously-skip-permissions` with `--permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob,Bash(git diff *)"`.
options.C: Keep `--dangerously-skip-permissions` and add `--disallowedTools "Edit" "Write"` to the `claude -p` review command.
options.D: Keep `--dangerously-skip-permissions` and add a PostToolUse hook that runs `git checkout .` after every tool call.

questions.explanation: B is correct. `--permission-mode dontAsk` auto-denies every call that would otherwise prompt, and `--allowedTools` pre-approves only reading and `git diff`. File edits, `npm install` and project scripts are therefore denied, while reads keep working and the unchanged JSON flags still produce `structured_output`. The permission-modes docs list this shape (dontAsk plus an exact `--allowedTools` list) for "Run in CI with an exact allowlist". C is the strongest near-miss: it uses the right kind of mechanism but blocks the wrong set of tools. Deny rules do apply even in bypassPermissions, so Edit and Write disappear. But Bash stays fully open, so `npm install`, project scripts and even `sed -i` edits still run. A is only an instruction the model reads, and with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` nothing stops a call Claude decides to make anyway. D reverts file edits only after they happen. It cannot undo a command that already ran, such as a package install or a script with side effects, and it leaves the bypass flag in place.

questions.stem: A nightly job on a shared CI virtual machine (not an isolated container) runs `claude -p "Run the unit tests and fix any failing tests"`. The run exits after a few turns with no files changed, and its log shows that every `Edit` call and every `npm test` call was denied. The job must be able to edit files and run `npm test` with nobody answering permission prompts, and any other command that changes files, installs packages, or runs project code must stay denied. Which invocation should the team use?

options.A: `claude -p "<prompt>" --dangerously-skip-permissions --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)"`
options.B: `claude -p "<prompt>" --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "Read,Edit"`
options.C: `claude -p "<prompt>" --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(npm test *)"`
options.D: `claude -p "<prompt>" --permission-mode auto --allowedTools "Bash(npm test *)"`

questions.explanation: C is correct. In `dontAsk` mode every call that would prompt is denied; only actions that never need approval (file reads, read-only commands) and actions the allow rules cover still run. The allowlist pre-approves exactly `Edit` and `npm test`, so the job runs unattended and every other state-changing command is denied. A is the strongest near-miss: its allowlist is correct, but it is paired with the wrong mode. `--dangerously-skip-permissions` equals `bypassPermissions`, and the docs state that "Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions", so every command runs. The docs also reserve that mode for isolated containers and VMs, which this shared VM is not. B approves file edits but has no entry for `npm test`, so the test runs are still denied and the fixes go unverified. D puts `auto` mode in charge, where a classifier model approves most actions. Commands beyond `npm test` can therefore run on the model's judgement, which is not an exact allowlist.

questions.stem: A CI step runs Claude Code after each merge to generate unit tests for the modules that changed. The prompt already includes each module's existing test file, and duplicate scenarios have stopped appearing. Reviewers still reject most generated tests: many assert only `expect(result).toBeDefined()` or that a mocked repository's `save` was called, and each test builds its own inline user objects instead of using the factories in `tests/fixtures/`. The project `CLAUDE.md` says only "Write thorough tests." What change most improves the generated tests?

options.A: Replace the `CLAUDE.md` line with test criteria: assert a specific outcome for each input, no existence-only or mock-call-only checks, build data with `tests/fixtures/`.
options.B: Add a CI gate that fails the step unless the generated tests raise line and branch coverage of the changed modules to at least 90 percent before merge.
options.C: Add a second, independent Claude review step that scores each generated test for usefulness and deletes every test it rates below a set threshold.
options.D: Change the `CLAUDE.md` line to "Write thorough, meaningful, high-quality tests; avoid trivial assertions and reuse existing helpers where possible."

questions.explanation: A is correct. The model already sees the existing tests. What it lacks is a definition of a valuable test in this project and the fixture convention. Guide 3.6 names this exact move: documenting testing standards, valuable test criteria and available fixtures in `CLAUDE.md` to improve generation quality and reduce low-value output. Concrete criteria give Claude a target it can check each test against: assert a specific outcome, existence-only or mock-call-only checks don't count, use `tests/fixtures/`. C is the strongest near-miss. Independent review is sound for code review, but this reviewer has no written criteria either, so it judges "usefulness" by the same vague notion. Deleting tests also leaves fewer tests, not better ones, because it filters the symptom after generation instead of defining the target before it. B rewards exactly the rejected tests, because `toBeDefined()` executes every line without checking any result. D is still the vague kind of instruction that produced the trivial tests: it never says what counts as meaningful, and "reuse existing helpers" doesn't name the fixtures.

questions.stem: A multi-agent research system receives the request: "Assess whether four-day school weeks improve academic outcomes in rural districts." The coordinator always runs the same four steps: a search subagent collects studies, an extraction subagent pulls test-score results from each study, an analysis subagent compares the results across districts, and a report subagent writes up the findings. In a test run, the search subagent reports that most of the 30 studies it found measure attendance, teacher retention, and budget savings rather than test scores, and that several districts reversed the policy after two years. The remaining steps run unchanged: extraction finds test-score data in only four studies, and the final report draws a strong conclusion from those four. What change to the coordinator would best address this?

options.A: Have the coordinator review each subagent's output before choosing what runs next, for example adding subtasks to find district test-score records outside the studies and to examine why districts reversed the policy.
options.B: Add a check after the extraction step that reruns the search with broader test-score keywords whenever fewer than ten studies report academic results, and then continues with the remaining steps.
options.C: Add an instruction to the report subagent to state how many studies support each conclusion and to add a caveat to any finding drawn from fewer than ten studies.
options.D: Run the search, extraction, and analysis subagents in parallel on separate slices of the topic, and then pass all of their outputs to the report subagent together for the write-up.

questions.explanation: A is correct. This is an open-ended research question, and the first step's findings showed that the plan's built-in assumption (the studies report test scores) was wrong and that a new line of inquiry (the policy reversals) matters. The defect is that the coordinator runs a fixed sequence regardless of intermediate findings. Having the coordinator read each result and generate the next subtasks from it (dynamic decomposition, the orchestrator-workers pattern for tasks whose subtasks cannot be predicted) lets the plan add work that no upfront plan contained. B fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 5, a symptom patch on the antipattern): it reacts to a bad result, so it looks adaptive, but it only repeats the same search under the assumption the finding just disproved, and the pipeline still cannot add a new kind of subtask such as investigating the reversals. C fails: stating sample sizes is good uncertainty practice, but it only describes the gap in the report; the missing investigation still never happens. D fails: parallelism changes how fast the fixed steps run, not what they are, so the plan still ignores what the search found.

questions.stem: A developer asks Claude Code to find everything that must change before the team replaces a deprecated ORM in a 300-module service. The first attempt used a fixed plan: Grep for modules that import the ORM, review each match, then write a report. The Grep found 40 modules. While reviewing them, the agent noticed that many other modules use the ORM without importing it: they inherit its query methods from a shared repository base class, and several call query code emitted at build time by a code generator. The report still covered only the 40 original matches. How should the task be decomposed on the next attempt?

options.A: Keep the Grep and review steps, and add a cross-module integration pass after the per-module reviews that checks how the 40 reviewed modules call into one another and share data.
options.B: Spawn one subagent per module for all 300 modules in parallel, each checking its own module for ORM usage, and then merge all of their reports into one list at the end.
options.C: First map how modules reach the database, including base classes and generated code, then create review subtasks from that map and add new ones when a review exposes another access path.
options.D: Ask the developer to provide a complete list of the modules that access the database, and then run the same Grep and review steps over that list instead of the Grep results.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The scope of this audit is unknown until the agent investigates: the first attempt already showed that ORM usage also arrives through a base class and generated code, which a keyword Grep for imports cannot find. An open-ended task like this needs dynamic decomposition: map the structure first, create subtasks from what the map reveals, and keep adding subtasks as reviews uncover new access paths. A fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 3, it treats a neighbouring problem): a per-file pass plus a cross-file integration pass is the right pattern for a predictable review of a known file set, where the risk is attention dilution. Here the problem is unknown scope, and an integration pass over the 40 matches still never examines the modules that inherit or generate their queries. B fails on proportionality and grounding: 300 subagents with no map are costly, each asks the same fixed question of its own slice, and the generator templates that emit the query code are nobody's subtask. D fails: discovering the scope is the task itself, and the developer did not know about these access paths either; the agent found them.

questions.stem: A pull-request review coordinator built with the Claude Agent SDK defines three subagents in the agents option: test-runner, dependency-auditor, and security-reviewer. The coordinator's allowedTools includes the Agent tool (formerly Task). Logs show the coordinator regularly spawns test-runner and dependency-auditor, but for pull requests that change authentication code it writes the security analysis itself, and no Agent tool call has ever used security-reviewer as its subagent_type. No errors are logged. The security-reviewer definition was created by copying the dependency-auditor definition; the team then rewrote its prompt field with detailed security-review instructions and left the other fields unchanged. What should the team change?

options.A: Add "security-reviewer" to the coordinator's allowedTools list next to the Agent tool, and restart the coordinator so that the updated list is loaded.
options.B: Rewrite security-reviewer's description to say what it reviews and when to use it, such as changes to authentication, session, or input-validation code.
options.C: Add to security-reviewer's prompt field a list of the file paths and change types it should handle, such as authentication, session, and input-validation code.
options.D: Give security-reviewer its own tools list with Read, Grep, and Glob in place of the tool settings it took over from the copied dependency-auditor definition.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The copied definition still carries dependency-auditor's description, and Claude decides which subagent to invoke by matching the task against each subagent's description (the SDK docs: write clear, specific descriptions so Claude can match tasks to the right subagent). Rewriting the description to state what the subagent handles and when to use it fixes the selection. C fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 2, right configuration object, wrong field): the prompt field is the subagent's own system prompt, which it reads only after it has been spawned, so more detail there cannot make the coordinator choose it. A fails: allowedTools lists tools, not subagents, and the logs already show the Agent tool working for the other two subagents. D fails: the tools list controls what the subagent can do once it runs, and this subagent is never spawned in the first place.

questions.stem: A nightly multi-agent pipeline audits 60 service repositories for license compliance. A coordinator assigns each repository to a scanner subagent, which returns its findings as the Agent tool result, and a report subagent combines all findings at the end. Last night the host restarted after 38 repositories had been scanned. The coordinator tracked which repositories were finished only in its own conversation, which had been auto-compacted twice during the run, condensing the early per-repository findings into short summaries. The team wants future interrupted runs to continue without rescanning finished repositories or losing any of their findings. What should they implement?

options.A: Save the coordinator's session ID when each run starts and, after an interruption, resume that session with the same agent definitions so it continues from its restored conversation history.
options.B: Raise the run's turn limit, move the job to a host with no scheduled restarts, and rerun all 60 repositories from the beginning whenever a run is interrupted before it completes.
options.C: Export the coordinator's full conversation transcript to disk after every ten repositories, and on restart load the latest export as the first message of a new coordinator session.
options.D: Have each scanner write its findings to a per-repository file and mark the repository done in a manifest that the coordinator loads on restart and injects into new subagent prompts.

questions.explanation: D is correct. It is the structured state persistence pattern for crash recovery: each agent exports its state to a known location, and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and injects the relevant state into agent prompts. Finished repositories are skipped because the manifest records them as done, and no finding is lost because each one lives in its own file rather than in a conversation that compaction can condense. A fails and is the strongest near-miss (axis 5, using the conversation as the state store): resuming does restore the session, but that conversation had already been auto-compacted, so the early per-repository findings survive only as short summaries, and there is no machine-readable record of which repositories are finished. C fails: it writes to disk, but it saves verbose transcript instead of structured per-repository state, loses up to nine repositories of work since the last export, and pushes the whole transcript back into the new context. B fails the stated goal directly: it rescans finished repositories, and neither a higher turn limit nor a different host prevents the next interruption.

questions.stem: A support agent for an electronics retailer keeps requests small with a sliding window that sends only the most recent 20 turns. In turn 3 of a long chat, the agent confirmed a $40 goodwill credit on order #55120 and promised free return shipping. At turn 34 the customer asks whether the credit has been applied. The agent replies that it has no record of any credit and offers to open a new request. Logs show the model never saw turn 3. What change most reliably prevents this failure while keeping requests small?

options.A: Enlarge the window to the most recent 50 turns, which covers the length of nearly all support chats in the logs.
options.B: Summarize each turn as it leaves the window into a running narrative that is sent ahead of the windowed turns.
options.C: Maintain a structured case-state object that the application updates after each turn and sends with every request.
options.D: Add a tool the agent can call to search the stored full transcript when the customer refers to something said earlier.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The failure happened because an exact commitment (a $40 credit on order #55120, plus free return shipping) existed only inside a turn that the window later dropped. A structured case-state object (order IDs, amounts, commitments, statuses) stores those facts outside the turns, keeps them exact, and is sent with every request. The window can keep cutting old turns, so requests stay small. B is the strongest near-miss. It is the known antipattern of progressive summarization for transactional data: a running summary keeps 'something', but it tends to shrink the credit into a phrase like 'offered a goodwill gesture', and the customer is asking exactly about that credit and whether it was applied. A only delays the problem: a chat longer than 50 turns drops turn 3 again, every request grows (breaking the 'keep requests small' condition), and nothing guarantees the commitment survives. D depends on the agent deciding to search. An agent that never saw turn 3 does not know a credit exists, so it has no reason to look, which is exactly why it answered 'no record'. Retrieval also adds a tool call to every such turn.

questions.stem: A developer-productivity agent monitors a long-running deployment. Every two minutes it calls get_deploy_status, which returns a ~3,000-token snapshot of the whole rollout (per-host state, recent log lines, health checks). Each new snapshot fully supersedes the previous one. Engineers only ask about the current state ("Is eu-west healthy now?"), and no answer depends on earlier snapshots. After six hours the request carries about 180 snapshots. Latency and cost have climbed, and answers sometimes quote a host state from an hour ago. What is the most effective change?

options.A: Keep only the latest few get_deploy_status results in the request and replace older snapshot results with a short placeholder.
options.B: Extract every host state and error from each snapshot into a running structured state object that is sent with every request.
options.C: Summarize older snapshots into a running narrative of the rollout history and keep only the most recent snapshot verbatim.
options.D: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window so all snapshots of a long rollout fit without truncation.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The stem says each snapshot fully supersedes the previous one and no answer depends on earlier snapshots. So the old tool results are pure cost and a source of stale answers. Keeping only the most recent few (a sliding window over tool results, or selective retention) removes both problems with the least machinery. The Claude API offers the same thing server-side as tool-result clearing (a beta strategy with a keep setting), which clears the oldest tool results first and replaces them with a placeholder. B is the strongest near-miss. A structured state object is the right tool when facts must survive exactly, but here nothing from old snapshots must survive. A running record built from every snapshot keeps growing, keeps superseded host states the engineers never ask about, and adds extraction work on every poll: the right idea, far too heavy for the job. C also keeps history nobody needs, costs a summarization call, and the narrative can still carry an hour-old host state into answers. D is the known antipattern: a bigger window keeps all 180 stale snapshots in the request, so cost and latency stay high, and it does nothing about answers quoting old states.
